items.title: The Sufuria Volcano
stuff: Half a cup of siki (vinegar) or juice from 2 ndimu
An old sufuria or a plastic bottle
Ink from a red or blue biro (break the tube open into a spoon of water)
steps: Stand the bottle in the middle of the sufuria so the mess stays inside.
Put the baking soda into the bottle.
Add the squeeze of dish soap and a few drops of the red colour.
Pour the siki in fast and step back.
Watch the foam climb up and pour over the sides like lava.
items.why: Baking soda is a base and siki is an acid. When they meet they swap parts and make carbon dioxide gas. The gas needs somewhere to go, so it pushes up through the soap and turns into thousands of tiny bubbles — foam.
items.care: Keep it out of your eyes. Siki stings.
items.twist: Try warm siki, then cold siki. Which one erupts higher? Time both with a phone.

items.title: Make Electricity From a Ndimu
stuff: A galvanised nail or a straightened paper clip, one for each fruit
A short piece of bare copper wire for each fruit — strip it from an old phone charger cable or a dead earphone
Thin wire to join them up, from the same old cable
A small LED bulb (from a dead torch, a broken toy, or a 50-bob torch from the duka)
steps: Roll each ndimu hard on the table to get the juice moving inside.
Ask an adult to strip the plastic off an old charger cable. The shiny orange strands inside are the copper.
Push a nail into one side of each ndimu and a bundle of copper strands into the other side. Do not let them touch.
Join the nail of the first ndimu to the copper of the second with a wire. Keep going until they are all in a chain.
Touch the two legs of the LED to the free nail and the free copper at the ends. Swap the legs round if nothing happens.
items.why: The juice inside a ndimu is acid. It pulls tiny bits called electrons off the nail and pushes them towards the copper. That flow of electrons is electricity. One ndimu is far too weak, so you line four up in a chain and add their pushes together.
items.care: Only an adult strips the cable, and only from something already thrown away and unplugged.
items.twist: Try potatoes, then tomatoes, then a mango. Make a chart of which one lights the bulb brightest. Kenyan coins will not work in place of the copper wire — they are steel with a thin coat, so test one and see for yourself.

items.title: Turmeric Spy Detector
stuff: Half a cup of warm water
A brush or a cotton bud
Things to test: siki, baking soda, soap, ndimu juice, Omo powder, sugar, chumvi
steps: Mix the turmeric into half a cup of warm water and stir hard. It goes bright yellow.
Paint the yellow liquid all over a sheet of white paper and let it dry. Now you have detector paper.
Dip the cotton bud in one thing you want to test and draw a line on the paper.
Watch the line. Bright red or deep orange means a base. Staying yellow means an acid or neither.
Test everything on your list and write down which is which.
items.why: Turmeric holds a yellow dye called curcumin. When a base touches it, the dye changes shape and starts bouncing back red light instead of yellow. Acids leave it alone, so it stays yellow. That is exactly what scientists mean by an indicator.
items.care: Turmeric stains everything it touches, including the table and your clothes. Cover the table with newspaper first.
items.twist: Write a secret message on plain paper with baking soda water, let it dry, then paint over it with the turmeric mix. The message appears in red.

items.title: The Egg That Loses Its Shell
stuff: Enough siki (vinegar) to cover the egg
steps: Put the raw egg gently into the glass.
Pour siki over it until the egg is fully covered.
Look at the little bubbles forming on the shell straight away.
Leave it for 2 days. Do not touch it.
Rinse it under the tap and rub the white shell off. You now have a see-through bouncy egg.
items.why: Egg shell is made of calcium carbonate. Siki is an acid that eats calcium carbonate and turns it into carbon dioxide — those are the bubbles. Underneath the shell there is a stretchy skin called a membrane, and that skin is what is left holding the egg together.
items.care: Bounce it low over a plate. It will burst if you throw it hard, and raw egg is messy.
items.twist: Put your naked egg in plain water overnight. It swells up. Put another one in very salty water. It shrinks. That is osmosis.

items.title: Make an Egg Float in the Middle
steps: Fill the glass halfway with water and drop the egg in. It sinks.
Take the egg out. Stir in 6 heaped spoons of salt until it dissolves.
Put the egg back. It floats.
Now very slowly pour plain water down the inside wall of the glass so it sits on top without mixing.
The egg will hang in the middle, trapped between the two waters.
items.why: Salty water is heavier than the same amount of plain water because the salt is packed in between. The egg is heavier than plain water but lighter than salty water, so it stops exactly where the two layers meet.
items.twist: This is why swimming is easier in the sea than in a pool. Explain that to someone at supper.

items.title: Rainbow Tower in a Glass
stuff: Thick sugar syrup — 4 spoons of sukari stirred into 1 spoon of hot water until it will take no more
Water with ink from a biro stirred into it
Small light things: a bottle top, a grape, a small stone, a pin
steps: Ask an adult for a spoon of hot water. Stir in sugar, a spoon at a time, until no more will dissolve. Let it cool.
Pour the sugar syrup straight into the bottom of the glass.
Pour dish soap slowly on top of the syrup, right in the centre.
Tilt the glass and pour the inky water gently down the side, then the oil the same way.
Drop your small objects in one by one and see which layer each one stops at.
items.why: Every liquid has a density — how much stuff is squeezed into the same space. The sugar syrup is heaviest because it has sugar packed into the gaps between the water. Heavy layers sink, light ones float, so they stack up in order without mixing. Your objects park on the layer that matches them.
items.twist: Make a second syrup with only half the sugar and build the tower again. It sits in a different place in the stack. Draw both and label them heaviest to lightest.

items.title: Dancing Milk
stuff: Ink from 3 different coloured biro pens, each squeezed into a spoon of water
A cotton bud or the tip of a matchstick
steps: Pour milk into the plate until the bottom is just covered. Let it go still.
Drop small dots of different colours near the middle. Do not stir.
Dip the cotton bud into dish soap.
Touch the soapy tip into the middle of one colour dot and hold it there.
Watch the colours run away from your bud and swirl.
items.why: Milk has tiny drops of fat floating in it, all holding hands on the surface. Soap breaks those bonds. The surface suddenly gets pulled around as the soap spreads, and the colours ride along like leaves on moving water.
items.twist: Try it again with water instead of milk. Almost nothing happens — that proves the fat is the important part.

items.title: Secret Message in Ndimu Juice
stuff: Juice of 1 ndimu in a small bowl
A cotton bud, a matchstick, or a thin brush
A source of gentle heat: a warm iron, a bulb, or sunshine on a hot day
steps: Squeeze the ndimu juice into the bowl and add 3 drops of water.
Dip the cotton bud and write your secret message on the paper.
Let it dry completely. The paper will look blank.
Give it to someone with the instruction to warm it.
Ask an adult to hold a warm iron over it, and the writing appears brown.
items.why: Ndimu juice soaks into the paper and dries clear. It burns at a lower temperature than paper does, so when you add gentle heat the juice browns first while the paper stays white. The message appears.
items.care: The iron is an adult job, always.
items.twist: Try the same thing with milk, and with onion juice. Which one shows up clearest?

items.title: Bottle Fountain With No Pump
stuff: A 500ml plastic bottle with its cap
Chewing gum or candle wax to seal
steps: Ask an adult to make a hole in the bottle cap just big enough for the straw.
Fill the bottle three-quarters with water.
Push the straw through the cap so the bottom end sits in the water and the top sticks out high.
Seal all around the straw and the hole so no air can sneak through.
Squeeze the bottle hard. Water shoots up the straw like a fountain.
items.why: When you squeeze, the air trapped above the water gets pressed into a smaller space, so it pushes harder on everything. The only escape route is the straw, so the water is forced up it. Let go and the air relaxes and the fountain drops.
items.twist: Use a thinner straw. The fountain goes higher because the same push is squeezed through a smaller opening.

items.title: Balloon Rocket on a String
stuff: String or washing line, about 5 metres
Two chairs or a door handle and a chair
steps: Thread the string through the straw.
Tie one end of the string to a chair and the other end across the room. Pull it tight.
Blow the balloon up but do not tie it. Pinch the neck shut.
Tape the balloon to the straw with the neck facing the chair you are standing next to.
Let go and watch it fly to the other end.
items.why: The air rushes out backwards, and the balloon is pushed forwards by the same amount. Every push has an equal push in the opposite direction — that is Newton's third law. Real rockets do exactly this with hot gas instead of air.
items.twist: Race two balloons on two strings. Does a fatter balloon beat a longer one? Test it three times before you decide.

items.title: Paper Helicopter Drop Test
stuff: An old exercise book page or newspaper
A paper clip or a small piece of ruba (rubber band)
Somewhere high but safe to drop from
steps: Cut a strip of paper about 4cm wide and 20cm long.
Cut a slit halfway down from the top, making two flaps. Fold one flap forward and one backward — these are the blades.
Fold the bottom third up and clip it with the paper clip to add weight.
Hold it as high as you can and let it go.
Time how long it takes to land. Do it 3 times and take the middle time.
items.why: Air pushes back on the tilted blades as the helicopter falls. That push spins it, and spinning slows the fall. This is how a maple seed and a real helicopter's autorotation both work.
items.twist: Add a second paper clip. Does it fall faster or slower? Now cut the blades shorter and test again. Record everything.

items.title: Make a Cloud in a Jar
stuff: A glass jar with a lid or a plate to cover it
steps: Pour hot water into the jar until it is a third full. Swirl it around to warm the glass, then leave it.
Put the lid upside down on top of the jar and pile ice cubes on the lid.
Ask an adult to light a match, blow it out, and drop the smoking match into the jar for one second, then cover it again quickly.
Watch inside the jar.
Lift the lid and let your cloud escape.
items.why: Hot water makes invisible water vapour rise. The ice makes the top of the jar cold, so the vapour cools down and turns back into tiny water drops. Those drops need something to stick to, and the smoke gives them that. Real clouds form on dust exactly the same way.
items.care: Adult handles the hot water and the match.
items.twist: Try it with no smoke at all. The cloud is much thinner — proof that clouds need dust.

items.title: Rain Cloud in a Glass
stuff: A clear glass of water, nearly full
A thick pile of cotton wool, or shaving foam if there is any
Ink from a blue biro, mixed into a little water
steps: Fill the glass with water, leaving 3cm at the top.
Pile cotton wool on top to make a fat cloud.
Let it settle for a minute.
Drop the blue coloured water onto the cloud, one spoonful at a time.
Keep going and watch the blue break through and rain down.
items.why: The foam holds the water like a real cloud holds water droplets. A cloud can only hold so much. When it gets too heavy, gravity wins and the water falls through as rain.
items.twist: Count how many spoonfuls your cloud can hold before it rains. Make a bigger cloud and count again.

items.title: Bend Water Without Touching It
stuff: A plastic comb, or an inflated balloon
A dry woollen sweater or your own hair
A tap running in a very thin stream
steps: Rub the comb through your dry hair 20 times, fast.
Hold it just above the torn paper bits and watch them jump up to it.
Now open the tap so a very thin, smooth stream of water runs.
Bring the charged comb close to the stream without touching it.
The water bends towards the comb.
items.why: Rubbing moves invisible electric charges onto the comb. Water molecules have a slightly positive end and a slightly negative end, so they turn to face the comb and get pulled sideways. This is static electricity — the same thing as the shock you feel from a car door.
items.twist: It works badly on a rainy day. Test it in the morning and in the evening and work out why humidity ruins it.

items.title: Lava Lamp in a Bottle
stuff: A clear plastic bottle or a tall glass
A fizzy tablet (Eno, Andrews, or a soluble painkiller — ask an adult first)
steps: Fill the bottle a quarter full with water.
Top it up to almost full with cooking oil. Wait for the two to separate.
Add 8 drops of colour. They fall through the oil and join the water.
Break the fizzy tablet into 4 pieces and drop one piece in.
Turn off the lights and shine a torch through it.
items.why: Oil and water do not mix because their molecules do not stick to each other. The tablet fizzes in the water and makes gas bubbles that carry blobs of coloured water up. At the top the gas escapes, the blob gets heavy again and sinks. Up and down forever.
items.care: Do not drink it. Do not eat the tablet.
items.twist: Add a second piece of tablet while the first is still going. Does it get faster or just messier?

items.title: Split a Pen Colour Into Its Secrets
stuff: White tissue or kitchen towel, or a strip cut from a white exercise book page
Water-based felt pens or markers, especially black and green
steps: Cut a strip of the paper about 3cm wide and 12cm long.
Draw a fat dot of black pen about 2cm from one end. Make it dark.
Tape the other end to a pencil and rest the pencil across the dish so the strip's bottom edge just touches the water. The dot must stay ABOVE the water.
Wait and watch the water climb up the paper.
When the colours have spread out, take it out and dry it.
items.why: Black ink is not one colour, it is a mixture. Water climbs the paper and drags the colours with it, but heavy colours get stuck near the bottom while light ones travel far. They separate into stripes. Scientists call this chromatography and use it to test medicines and even crime scenes.
items.twist: Test 5 different black pens. Every brand makes a different stripe pattern — like a fingerprint. Could you catch a forger with this?

items.title: Grow Your Own Crystals
stuff: Chumvi (salt) or sugar — lots of it
A piece of thread or sisal string
A pencil and a paper clip
steps: Ask an adult to make a cup of very hot water.
Stir in salt one spoon at a time and keep stirring. Stop when no more will dissolve and grains sit at the bottom.
Pour the clear liquid into the jar, leaving the leftover grains behind.
Tie the thread to the pencil, tie a paper clip to the bottom for weight, and hang it in the water. Rest the pencil across the jar rim.
Put it somewhere still and do not touch it. Check it every day for a week.
items.why: Hot water can hold much more salt than cold water. As the water cools and slowly evaporates, there is no longer room for all that salt, so it comes out of the water and locks itself onto the string in neat repeating shapes. Those shapes are crystals — the same way real gemstones form underground, just much faster.
items.care: Adult handles the hot water.
items.twist: Do salt in one jar and sugar in another. Look at both under a magnifying glass. Salt makes cubes. Sugar makes long slanted blocks. Draw both.

items.title: Watch a Plant Drink
stuff: A thick sukuma wiki stem, or a white flower, or a spring onion
Ink from a blue biro, mixed into a little water
steps: Mix a lot of colour into the glass of water — much more than looks sensible.
Ask an adult to cut the very bottom off the stem so it is fresh.
Stand the stem in the coloured water.
Leave it for a few hours. Check it after 2 hours, then after a whole day.
Ask an adult to cut across the stem and look at the coloured dots inside.
items.why: Plants have tiny straws running up their stems called xylem. Water climbs them because water molecules stick to each other and to the tube walls, and because water leaving the leaves pulls the rest up behind it. The dye tags along so you can see the route.
items.twist: Split the bottom of one stem into two and put each half in a different colour. You get a two-coloured plant.

items.title: Bean Farm in a Jar
stuff: Cotton wool, or scrunched tissue paper
steps: Pack the cotton wool loosely into the jar until it is nearly full.
Push the beans down the SIDE of the jar so you can see them through the glass, halfway down.
Pour in water until the cotton is properly damp but not swimming.
Put the jar somewhere with light and keep the cotton damp every day.
Draw what you see every single day for 10 days. Do not skip a day.
items.why: A dry bean is a sleeping plant with its own packed lunch inside. Water wakes it up. The root always grows down and the shoot always grows up, even in the dark — the seed can sense gravity. Your drawings will show the root appearing first, because a plant needs a drink before anything else.
items.twist: Turn one jar completely upside down on day 4. The root will curve around and head back down within two days. Photograph it.

items.title: The Water Cycle in a Bag
steps: Draw a sun, a cloud and some waves on the outside of the bag with the marker.
Pour in a small amount of blue water — about 3cm deep — and seal the bag tightly.
Tape the bag to the inside of a window that gets strong sun.
Check it after 2 hours and again in the evening.
You will see drops on the inside walls that slide back down.
items.why: Sun heats the water so it evaporates into invisible vapour. The vapour hits the cooler top of the bag, cools, and condenses back into drops. When the drops get heavy they run down — that is precipitation. The whole world's rain works on this loop, just much bigger.
items.twist: Tape a second bag to a shaded window. Compare after one day. That difference is why the coast is more humid than the highlands.

items.title: Build a Sundial and Beat the Clock
stuff: A flat sunny patch of ground or a big sheet of paper on a table outside
A watch or phone for the time
steps: Push the stick upright into the ground in a spot that gets sun all day.
At 9:00 exactly, put a stone where the tip of the shadow falls. Write 9 on it with chalk.
Do the same every hour: 10, 11, 12, 1, 2, 3, 4.
The next morning, use only the shadow and your stones to tell someone the time.
Check against a real clock and see how close you got.
items.why: The Earth spins once a day, so the sun appears to move across the sky. The shadow swings the opposite way at a steady rate. Before clocks existed, this is how the whole world told the time.
items.twist: Mark the shadow tip at noon, then do it again a month later at noon. It will have moved. That is because the Earth is tilted, and that tilt is what makes seasons.

items.title: Floating Compass
stuff: A sewing needle or a straightened paper clip
A magnet — from broken earphones, an old speaker, a fridge magnet, or a broken toy
A leaf, a bottle top, or a small piece of cork
A real compass or a phone compass to check
steps: Stroke the needle with one end of the magnet, always in the SAME direction, 40 times. Lift the magnet away between strokes.
Test it by seeing if the needle now picks up a paper clip.
Lay the needle on the leaf or push it through the bottle top so it floats flat.
Float it in the middle of the bowl of water and let it settle.
It will turn and point north and south. Check with a phone compass.
items.why: Stroking lines up the tiny magnetic bits inside the steel so they all face the same way, which turns the needle into a magnet. The Earth itself is a giant weak magnet, so your floating needle turns until it lines up with it. Sailors crossed oceans with nothing better than this.
items.twist: Bring the magnet near the floating needle and watch it swing. Now you know why you must never keep a compass next to a phone speaker.

items.title: Oobleck: Solid and Liquid at Once
stuff: 1 cup cornflour (unga wa maize starch), or plain unga if that is what you have
Ink from a biro, if you want it coloured
steps: Put the cornflour in the bowl.
Add the water a little at a time, mixing with your hands, not a spoon.
Stop when it pours like cream but goes hard the moment you tap it.
Punch it fast. It feels solid. Now rest your finger on it slowly. It swallows your finger.
Roll a ball in your palms, then stop moving — it melts back into liquid.
items.why: The unga grains are floating in water. When you hit it fast, the grains have no time to move out of the way, so they jam together and act like a solid. Slowly, they slide past each other and behave like a liquid. Scientists call this a non-Newtonian fluid.
items.care: Wash it down the sink with plenty of water, or it blocks the drain.
items.twist: Put some on a speaker playing loud bass and watch it dance. Or make a big tray of it and try to run across.

items.title: Egg Drop Challenge
stuff: Raw eggs (3 or 4, so you can lose some)
Newspaper, old cloth, cotton wool, straws, a polythene bag, sellotape, kamba
Somewhere to drop from safely, like a first-floor window or standing on a chair outside
steps: Design a container that will keep an egg alive from a big drop. Draw your plan first.
Build it. You are allowed a parachute from a polythene bag and string, padding, or a straw cage — or all three.
Drop it from standing height first. If the egg survives, go higher.
Write down what broke and why.
Rebuild and beat your own record.
items.why: The egg breaks because it stops too suddenly. Padding and parachutes both make the stop take longer, and a slower stop means a gentler force. This is exactly why cars have crumple zones and airbags.
items.care: Drop outside, over grass or soil. Never drop where someone might walk. Wash your hands after handling raw egg.
items.twist: Challenge a friend or cousin. Same materials, same height. Best design wins.

items.title: Tornado in Two Bottles
stuff: A drop of dish soap and some tiny torn paper bits
steps: Fill one bottle two-thirds with water. Add the soap and paper bits.
Stand the empty bottle upside down, mouth to mouth on top of the full one.
Tape the two necks together very tightly, going round and round many times. No leaks.
Flip it so the full bottle is on top.
Swirl it hard in a circle and then hold it still. Watch the tornado form.
items.why: Water falling straight down has to fight the air trying to come up the same hole, so it glugs. When you spin it, the water swirls to the outside and leaves a clear hole in the middle for the air to travel up. That spinning funnel is a vortex — a small version of a real tornado or the swirl in a bath drain.
items.twist: Time how long it takes to empty with a swirl versus without a swirl. The swirl is much faster.

items.title: Solar Water Heater
stuff: Black paint, a black polythene bag, or black paper
A thermometer if you have one, or just your hand
steps: Wrap one bottle completely in black. Leave the other one clear.
Fill both with exactly the same amount of cold water from the same tap.
Put them side by side in full sun at 10am.
Come back after 1 hour and feel both. Then again after 3 hours.
Write down which is hotter and by how much.
items.why: Black surfaces absorb almost all the light that hits them and turn it into heat. Shiny and clear surfaces let light pass through or bounce it away. This is why a black car gets unbearable in Nairobi sun and why solar water heaters on roofs are always black.
items.twist: Add a third bottle wrapped in foil. Rank all three. Now you can explain why people wear light colours in hot weather.

items.title: Bottle Top Mosaic Name Sign
stuff: Lots of soda bottle tops, washed
A piece of cardboard from a box
Glue (or make the flour glue, idea c05)
steps: Cut the cardboard into a rectangle big enough for your name.
Pencil your name in fat bubble letters, edge to edge.
Paint the bottle tops in two or three colours and let them dry — one colour for the letters, another for the background.
Glue tops along your pencil lines first, then fill the background.
Let it dry flat overnight, then hang it on your door.
items.why: This is mosaic — a real art form thousands of years old where a picture is built from many small pieces. Up close you see bottle tops. From across the room your brain fills in the gaps and you see a word.
items.twist: Make one for someone else as a gift, in their favourite colours.

items.title: Weave a Basket From Newspaper
stuff: A pencil or a thin straight stick
A bowl or tin to shape it around
steps: Cut newspaper into strips about 8cm wide.
Lay the stick at one corner of a strip and roll the paper tightly around it at an angle. Glue the last corner and slide the stick out. You now have a paper tube. Make about 40 of them.
Lay 8 tubes flat side by side, then weave 8 more across them over-under, over-under, to make a flat square base.
Turn the loose ends upward around your bowl and weave new tubes around and around the sides, joining tubes by pushing one into the end of another.
Fold the top ends over and tuck them in. Paint it or leave it as newsprint.
items.why: Weaving works because over-under-over-under locks the strands so friction holds everything without any glue. It is the same structure as a kiondo, a fishing net and the cloth you are wearing right now.
items.twist: Look closely at a real kiondo or a mkeka and copy its pattern instead of plain over-under.

items.title: Sisal Rope Coasters
stuff: Thick string, washing line, or kamba, about 3 metres per coaster
steps: Cut a circle of cardboard the size of a cup base.
Put a line of glue in a spiral on the cardboard, starting at the centre.
Coil the string tightly around itself onto the glue, pressing as you go. Keep it flat.
Keep coiling until you reach the edge of the cardboard, then cut and glue the end down neatly.
Press a book on top for an hour while it dries.
items.why: A coil spiral is one of the strongest flat shapes you can make from a single line — no joins, no weak points. Potters build pots this way with rolls of clay.
items.twist: Dye half your string with tea, beetroot or turmeric water first, and make a two-tone spiral.

items.title: Papier-Mache Bowl
stuff: A bowl to use as a mould
A polythene bag, or a smear of cooking oil
steps: Turn the bowl upside down and cover the outside with a polythene bag or rub oil on it, so your paper will come off later.
Dip a newspaper strip into the flour glue, run it between two fingers to wipe off the extra, and lay it on the bowl.
Cover the whole bowl, overlapping strips in every direction. That is layer one.
Do 4 more layers, drying properly between each one. Rushing this is why bowls collapse.
When completely hard and dry, gently pull it off the mould, trim the rim with scissors, and paint it.
items.why: Wet paper fibres swell and tangle. As the glue dries it locks all those tangled fibres into one stiff sheet. Layering in different directions makes it strong in every direction — the same trick as plywood and fibreglass.
items.twist: Do the last layer with plain white paper so your paint colours come out bright instead of grey.

items.title: Make Glue From Unga
stuff: Half a cup of unga (wheat flour)
steps: Mix the flour and cold water in the sufuria until there are no lumps at all. Lumps now means lumps forever.
Ask an adult to heat it on low, stirring the whole time.
When it thickens into a smooth paste like porridge, take it off the heat.
Let it cool completely. It thickens more as it cools.
Store it in the jar. It keeps for about 4 days, or a week in the fridge.
items.why: Flour is full of starch. Heat makes starch grains burst open and their long molecules tangle together into a sticky mesh. When the water dries out, the mesh grips both surfaces. This is genuinely how books were bound for centuries.
items.care: Adult at the cooker. Add a pinch of salt to stop it going mouldy so fast.
items.twist: This is the glue for papier-mache, paper beads and collage. Make a big batch before a craft afternoon.

items.title: Cardboard Roller Prints
stuff: A strip of corrugated cardboard, torn so the wavy ridges inside show
An empty tin or a bottle to wrap it around
Paint, or thick colour made from turmeric, tea or soot mixed with a little water and flour glue
A flat plate for the paint
Bottle tops and a cut potato for extra stamps
steps: Tear the top layer off a piece of cardboard so the wavy ridges underneath are showing.
Wrap that strip around a tin or bottle, ridges facing out, and tape it on. This is your roller.
Pour a thin layer of paint onto the plate and spread it flat.
Roll the tin through the paint until the ridges are covered, then roll it across your paper in one steady movement without stopping.
Reload and roll another line right next to the first until the whole sheet is covered.
items.why: The ridges touch the paper and the grooves between them do not, so the cardboard's own texture becomes your pattern. Every printed thing you own — books, kanga, money — is made the same way, by ink touching some places and not others.
items.twist: Press a bottle top into the paint and stamp circles between the lines. Then ask an adult to cut a potato in half, carve a shape into the flat face, and stamp with that too.

items.title: Avocado Seed Creatures
stuff: Avocado seeds, washed and dried for a day
Scraps: paper, wool, bottle tops, seeds for eyes
steps: Wash the seeds and let them dry properly. Wet seeds will not hold paint.
Decide what each seed will become — an owl, a fish, a monster, a bug.
Paint the base colour and let it dry fully before adding details.
Glue on wool for hair, paper for wings and ears, seeds or beads for eyes.
Line them up on a shelf as a family.
items.why: An avocado seed is smooth, hard and already egg-shaped, which is why it takes paint well and looks like a body without you doing anything. Artists call this working with the material instead of against it.
items.twist: Take one clean seed, stick 3 toothpicks in its side, and balance it in a glass so the fat end sits in water. In 3 to 6 weeks it splits and grows an avocado tree. Start it today.

items.title: Sock Puppet Theatre
stuff: Buttons or bottle tops for eyes
Wool or old string for hair
A cardboard box for the stage
steps: Put your hand in the sock and push your fingers into the toe to find where the mouth folds. That spot decides where the eyes go.
Sew or glue on the eyes above the fold.
Add wool hair, a felt tongue, ears, a hat — give this character a personality.
Cut a big rectangle out of one side of the cardboard box to make a stage window.
Write a short play with 2 puppets and perform it for the family.
items.why: Puppets work because of something called suspension of disbelief. Everyone can see it is a sock, but the moment it moves and talks, the brain treats it as alive. Movement and eyes are all it takes.
items.twist: Record the play on a phone and add sound effects made with kitchen things — rice in a tin for rain, a ruler twanged on a table for boing.

items.title: Paper Bead Necklace
stuff: A pencil, a thin stick, or a toothpick
Clear nail varnish or oil, if you have it
steps: Cut long triangles from the magazine pages: about 3cm wide at the base, going down to a point, and 20cm long. Bright, busy pages make the best beads.
Lay the stick across the wide end and roll the paper tightly around it, keeping it centred.
Put glue on the last 4cm and finish rolling. Hold for 10 seconds and slide the bead off.
Make 30 to 40 beads and let them dry.
Paint each with clear nail varnish to make them shiny and tough, then thread them onto the string.
items.why: Rolling a triangle instead of a rectangle is the whole trick — it makes the middle fatter than the ends, so you get a proper bead shape instead of a tube. Ugandan and Kenyan crafters sell these all over the world.
items.twist: Sort your beads by colour and make a repeating pattern instead of random. Patterns look far more expensive.

items.title: Matchbox Chest of Drawers
stuff: Beads, pins or small buttons for handles
steps: Push all the drawers out and set them aside.
Glue the outer shells together in a block — 3 across and 3 up makes a good chest. Let it dry properly.
Cover the outside with coloured paper or paint it.
Paint the drawers a different colour, then glue a bead on the front of each as a handle.
Slide the drawers back in and fill them with your tiny treasures.
items.why: Nine little boxes glued together are far stronger than one big box of the same size, because every shared wall braces the others. Engineers use this idea in bridges and aeroplane wings and call it a honeycomb structure.
items.twist: Label each drawer and use it as a real science kit: seeds, wires, magnets, crystals, coins.

items.title: Flashing Foil Wind Spinner
stuff: Bottle tops, beads, or old keys
A stick, or a wire clothes hanger
steps: Cut 4 circles of cardboard about the size of your palm.
Glue foil onto both sides of each circle, shiny side out, and smooth it flat with your thumb. Wrinkles are fine — they flash more.
Make a small hole near the edge of each circle and tie a different length of string to each so they do not knock into each other.
Tie the other ends along the stick, and hang bottle tops underneath so they clink in the wind.
Hang it outside where the morning sun hits it.
items.why: Foil is a mirror. A flat mirror sends light off in one direction, but your foil has hundreds of tiny bends, so each bend throws light a different way. As the wind turns the circles, different bends line up with the sun one after another and you see it flash. Farmers hang exactly this in shambas to startle birds off the crop.
items.twist: Take one circle into a dark room and shine a torch on it against the wall. Tilt it slowly and watch the bright patch jump around. Then squash a fresh piece of foil into a ball, open it out, and compare how much more it flashes.

items.title: Straw Domes and Towers
stuff: A small book or a stone to test the strength
steps: Make 6 triangles first by joining 3 straws end to end. Squeeze one straw's end and push it into the next.
Notice a triangle cannot be squashed out of shape, but a square can. Test both with your hands.
Join your triangles edge to edge, curving upward, to build a dome.
Build the tallest tower you can that still holds a book on top.
Measure your record and write it down, then try to beat it.
items.why: A triangle is the only shape that cannot change without a side breaking. Squares collapse into diamonds. That is why every crane, roof truss, bridge and pylon you have ever seen is full of triangles.
items.twist: Build one tower from triangles and one from squares, exactly the same height. Load them both with books until they fall. The result will not be close.

items.title: Cardboard Loom Weaving
stuff: Thread, wool, or old t-shirts cut into long strips
steps: Mark dots every 1cm along the top and bottom short edges of the cardboard. Cut a 1cm slit at each dot.
Slot the string into the first top slit, run it down to the matching bottom slit, around the back, and up again. Keep going until the whole board is strung. This is the warp.
Now weave a different colour across, over-under-over-under. At the end of the row, turn around and go back doing the opposite.
Push each row down snug with the fork.
When it is full, cut the loops at the back, tie pairs of loose ends together, and slide your weaving off.
items.why: Every piece of cloth in your house is exactly this: threads one way, threads the other way, locked by friction. You are doing by hand what a mill does thousands of times a second.
items.twist: Change colour every 5 rows for stripes, or weave in a feather, dry grass or a ribbon for texture.

items.title: Egg Carton Garden
stuff: A cardboard egg tray (the big 30-egg one)
Wire, straws or sticks for stems
Beads or seeds for flower centres
steps: Cut the tray into individual cups.
Trim the edge of each cup into 4, 5 or 6 petal shapes.
Squash them a bit to open the petals out, then paint them bright colours inside and out.
Push a straw or wire through the bottom for a stem and glue a bead in the centre.
Stand the bunch in a bottle as a vase that never dies.
items.why: A cardboard egg tray (the big 30-egg one) are moulded paper pulp — soft enough to cut but stiff enough to hold a curve when it dries. That is why the same material protects eggs and can become a petal.
items.twist: Instead of flowers, cut them into caterpillars: join 5 cups in a line, add wire or rolled paper antennae, and paint spots.

items.title: Punched Tin Lantern
stuff: A clean empty tin can with no sharp lid edges
An ordinary candle, or a small torch
steps: Fill the can with water and freeze it solid overnight. The ice stops the can bending when you hammer.
Draw your design on the outside with the marker — dots making a star, your initial, or a pattern.
Ask an adult to hammer the nail through the can on each dot, working on a towel so it does not roll.
Let the ice melt out and dry the can.
Twist a wire handle onto two holes at the top, paint the outside, and put a light inside.
items.why: Water expands when it freezes, so the ice presses outward on the can walls and supports them from inside. Without it, the tin would just crumple. Every hole becomes a beam of light in the dark.
items.care: The adult does the hammering. Tin edges are sharp — do not run your finger inside the can.
items.twist: Use a battery tea light instead of a flame and it is safe to keep in your room.

items.title: Bottle Planter and Watering Can
stuff: A knife or scissors (adult for the first cut)
Soil and seeds — beans, dhania, sukuma wiki, or a mango seed
steps: For the planter: ask an adult to cut a 2 litre bottle in half. Ask them to make 4 small holes in the bottom half for drainage.
Paint the outside — faces work well, so the plant becomes the hair.
Fill with soil and plant your seeds. Water lightly.
For the watering can: take a 500ml bottle with its cap on. Ask an adult to punch 8 tiny holes in the cap.
Fill it with water, screw the cap on, and tip it to sprinkle.
items.why: The drainage holes matter more than anything. Roots need air as much as water, and a pot with no holes drowns the plant. The watering can works because the small holes break one heavy stream into gentle drops that do not wash away seeds.
items.care: An adult makes every cut and every hole.
items.twist: Plant dhania and sukuma wiki, and keep a growth chart. When the dhania is ready, it goes into the family's food — grown by you.

items.title: Homemade Playdough
stuff: Natural colours: turmeric for yellow, beetroot juice for pink if you have one, soot from under a sufuria for grey, spinach juice for green
steps: Mix the flour and salt in a bowl.
Add the oil and water and mix into a dough with your hands.
Knead it on the table for 5 minutes until it is smooth and no longer sticky. Add a little flour if it sticks.
Split it into 3 or 4 balls and knead a different natural colour into each one.
Store each colour in a separate tight tin or bag. It lasts weeks.
items.why: The salt does two jobs: it makes the dough firm, and it stops mould growing by pulling water away from any bacteria. The oil keeps it soft and stops it drying out and cracking.
items.twist: Make small models, then leave them in strong sun for two days. They go hard like clay and you can paint them.

items.title: Rubber Band Guitar
stuff: An empty box — a shoe box, a tissue box, or a strong carton
5 or 6 rubber bands of different thicknesses
A cardboard tube for the neck, if you want
steps: Cut a round hole about 8cm across in the middle of the box lid.
Stretch the rubber bands around the whole box so they pass over the hole. Space them out.
Slide one pencil under all the bands at one end of the hole and another pencil at the other end. This lifts the bands off the box.
Pluck each band and listen.
Tape a cardboard tube on as a neck if you want it to look the part.
items.why: Plucking makes the band vibrate. The vibration shakes the air inside the box, and the box makes it much louder — that is why the hole matters. Thin, tight, short bands vibrate faster and sound higher. Thick, loose, long ones sound lower. That is all a guitar is.
items.twist: Slide one pencil closer to the other and pluck again — the note gets higher. You just made a fret. Try to find the notes of a song you know.

items.title: Kaleidoscope From a Tube
stuff: A cardboard tube (from kitchen foil, or rolled up from a cereal box)
Aluminium foil, as smooth as you can get it
Small colourful bits: beads, torn sweet wrappers, tiny snips of coloured paper
steps: Cut 3 strips of cardboard the length of the tube and as wide as a third of its width. Cover each one with foil, shiny side out and as smooth as you can get it.
Tape the 3 strips into a long triangle, shiny sides facing inward, and slide it into the tube.
Tape a clear plastic circle over one end of the tube.
Drop your beads and wrappers onto that plastic, then tape a second clear circle over them, leaving a small gap so they can tumble.
Cover the other end with cardboard with a small eye-hole in the middle. Point it at a light and turn.
items.why: Three mirrors in a triangle bounce the image of your beads off each other over and over. Each bounce makes another copy, and the copies arrange into a six-sided pattern. Nothing inside is symmetrical — the symmetry is created purely by the mirrors.
items.twist: Make a second one with 4 mirrors instead of 3. The pattern changes completely. Which do you prefer?

items.title: Bird Feeder From a Bottle
stuff: A 2 litre plastic bottle with a cap
Grain: millet, sorghum, or leftover rice and bread crumbs
steps: Ask an adult to cut two small holes opposite each other, low on the bottle, and two more higher up on the other two sides.
Push a stick through each pair of holes so it sticks out both sides. Those are perches, and the holes above them let seed trickle out.
Ask an adult to widen the hole just above each perch slightly so grain can escape.
Fill the bottle with grain through the top and screw the cap on.
Tie kamba around the neck and hang it in a tree where you can see it from a window.
items.why: Grain falls only as fast as birds take it, because the pile inside supports itself over a small hole — the same reason sand does not all pour out of an hourglass at once. The perches let birds sit and eat instead of hovering.
items.care: Keep it where cats cannot reach. Rinse it out every couple of weeks.
items.twist: Keep a bird notebook. Sketch every different bird that visits and count how many days each takes to find the feeder.

items.title: Make Paint From the Kitchen
stuff: Beetroot for deep pink, if there is one in the house
Spinach or sukuma wiki for green
Soot scraped from under a sufuria, or 5 burnt matchsticks crushed fine, for black
Small jars, water, and a little flour glue or oil to thicken
steps: For turmeric and soot: mix a spoon of powder with a little water in a jar until it is like thin cream.
For beetroot and spinach: grate them, squeeze the juice out through a cloth, and use the juice.
For tea: brew it very strong and let it cool.
Stir a small amount of flour glue into each one so the colour sticks to paper instead of soaking straight through.
Test each colour on a scrap first, then paint properly.
items.why: A paint is always two things: a pigment that gives colour, and a binder that glues it to the paper. Before paint was sold in shops, every artist made their own exactly like this, from plants, earth and soot.
items.care: Beetroot and turmeric stain badly. Wear an old t-shirt and cover the table.
items.twist: Paint the same picture twice — once with shop paint and once with kitchen paint. Which one do you actually prefer?

items.title: Shading With a Soft Pencil
stuff: A soft pencil — a B or 2B is best, but any pencil works if you press hard
A tissue or a bit of cotton wool
A round object: an orange, a ball, a mango
steps: Put the mango on the table where light hits it from one side only. Notice where it is brightest and where it is darkest.
Draw the outline lightly with the pencil.
Scribble all over the shape, then rub it smooth with the tissue until it looks like grey mist.
Go over the shadow side again, pressing harder each time. Add a shadow on the table underneath it too.
Use the rubber to LIFT the grey off where the light is brightest. That highlight is what makes it look round.
items.why: Your brain reads round shapes from light and shadow, not from lines. A circle with an outline stays a flat circle. Add a dark side, a light side and a shadow on the table, and the same circle becomes a ball. Rubbing out the highlight is drawing in reverse — you are drawing with light.
items.twist: A burnt matchstick, cooled, works just as well as a pencil and smudges even more easily. Try the same drawing with one and compare.

items.title: Blow Painting Trees
stuff: Watery paint or ink (thin it with water until it runs)
steps: Spoon a blob of runny dark paint near the bottom of the paper.
Put the straw close to the blob — but do NOT put the straw in your mouth over the paint — and blow hard, pushing the paint outward.
Blow from different angles to chase the paint into branching lines.
Keep chasing the thin ends and they will split into smaller and smaller branches.
When it is dry, add pink or yellow blossom with your fingertip.
items.why: The paint splits into branches on its own because air pushes it into the path of least resistance. Real trees, rivers, lightning and the veins in your hand all branch in the same pattern for the same reason — it is the most efficient way to spread out. Mathematicians call these fractals.
items.care: Blow, never suck.
items.twist: Take a photo of a real tree against the sky and hold it next to your blown painting. Compare the branching.

items.title: Rubbings Treasure Hunt
stuff: Crayons or a soft pencil with the point worn flat
Textured things around the house and outside: coins, leaves, tree bark, a brick wall, a sieve, a comb, a shoe sole, sisal mat
steps: Put the paper flat on top of a leaf, vein side up.
Hold the crayon on its SIDE, not its point, and rub firmly across the paper.
The texture appears like magic.
Go around the house and outside collecting 10 different textures on one big sheet, overlapping them.
Label each one in small writing — where you found it.
items.why: The crayon only touches the raised parts of whatever is under the paper. Dips stay blank. You are copying a 3D surface onto flat paper without ever seeing it. Archaeologists record ancient carvings with exactly this method.
items.twist: Make rubbings of coins and turn them into a picture — a robot made entirely of coin faces and sieve mesh.

items.title: Fold and Print Butterflies
steps: Fold a sheet of paper in half and open it flat again.
Spoon blobs of paint onto ONE side of the fold only. Do not spread them.
Fold the paper closed and press and smooth it with your hand from the fold outwards.
Open it. Both sides match exactly.
When dry, cut it into a butterfly or a moth shape and add antennae with a pen.
items.why: Pressing squashes the paint sideways into the empty half in a mirror image. This is symmetry. Butterflies, faces, leaves and your own body are all roughly symmetrical, which is one reason the result looks like a living thing rather than a mess.
items.twist: Try a fold down the middle and then a second fold across it, so you get four matching quarters. That is the pattern in a snowflake and a flower.

items.title: Grid Copy: Draw Anything Accurately
stuff: A photo you want to copy — printed, or on a phone screen
steps: Draw a grid of 2cm squares over your photo — on a printed copy, or on tracing paper laid over the screen.
Draw the SAME number of squares on your blank paper, but make each square 4cm instead of 2cm.
Pick one square in the photo. Ignore everything else in the world. Copy only the lines inside that one square.
Move to the next square. Never look at the whole picture while you draw.
When every square is done, rub out the grid lines. Your drawing will be twice the size and surprisingly accurate.
items.why: Your brain draws what it THINKS things look like — eyes too big, noses too small — instead of what is really there. Grids break the picture into shapes so small your brain cannot recognise them, so it stops interfering and you copy what your eyes actually see. Artists have used this since the 1400s.
items.twist: Do a portrait of someone in your family this way and give it to them. Try it once with the photo upside down — it is even more accurate, and that fact tells you something about brains.

items.title: One Line, Never Lift the Pen
stuff: A pen (not a pencil — no rubbing out allowed)
Something to draw: a hand, a shoe, a plant, a face
steps: Put the pen on the paper and promise not to lift it until you are finished.
Look at your subject far more than you look at the paper. Aim for 80 percent looking at the object.
Move the pen slowly, following the edges of what you see with your eyes and your hand at the same speed.
Do not rub out. Do not fix. Wrong lines stay.
Do 5 drawings of the same object this way, one after another.
items.why: Lifting the pen gives your brain a chance to take over and fake it. Keeping it down forces your hand to follow your eyes. Drawings 4 and 5 will be noticeably better than drawing 1 — that improvement is you learning to see instead of learning to draw.
items.twist: Try it without looking at the paper AT ALL. The result will be wild and strangely alive. Artists call this blind contour drawing and it is a real exercise, not a joke.

items.title: Map of Your World
stuff: A big sheet of paper, or two taped together
steps: Stand outside your gate and look around properly. Notice what is actually there.
Put your house in the middle of the paper.
Draw the road, the shops, the neighbours' houses, the big trees, the church or mosque, the school route, the place where the dog always barks.
Add a key in the corner explaining your symbols, and a compass arrow showing north — check with a phone or a shadow at noon.
Name the streets and paths yourself if they have no names.
items.why: A map is not a picture, it is a translation. You are converting a 3D world you walk through into a flat picture seen from above, which is something no one can actually see. Every map ever made is an act of imagination plus measurement.
items.twist: Add a second layer: mark in one colour everywhere you have been, and in another everywhere you have only heard about. Then go somewhere new and update it.

items.title: Shadow Tracing
stuff: Strong sunlight or a torch in a dark room
Small objects: toys, a plant, kitchen tools, your own hand
steps: Put the paper flat on the ground in strong sun, or on a table with a torch shining sideways.
Stand an object so its shadow falls across the paper.
Trace around the shadow with a pencil, keeping the object completely still.
Move the object and trace another shadow overlapping the first.
Colour each overlapping section a different colour, so it becomes an abstract pattern.
items.why: A shadow is a shape made of missing light. It shows an object's outline with all the detail stripped away, which is why shadows are the best way to learn silhouettes. Move the light and the same object gives a completely different shape.
items.twist: Trace your own shadow on the ground with chalk at 9am, noon and 4pm. It changes length dramatically. That is the sun's angle changing, and it is why the middle of the day is hottest.

items.title: Scratch Art Rainbow
stuff: One black crayon, or black paint mixed with a drop of dish soap
A pin, a paper clip, or a toothpick
steps: Colour the whole sheet in bright patches — press HARD so the wax goes on thick. No white gaps at all.
Now cover the entire sheet in solid black, either with a black crayon pressed hard or black paint with soap in it. Let it dry.
Scratch a drawing into the black with the pin.
Wherever you scratch, a bright colour appears from underneath.
Do a night scene — stars, fireworks, a city, a lion's eyes in the dark.
items.why: Wax is waterproof and slippery, so black paint sits on top instead of sinking in — the drop of soap is what lets it cling at all. Scratching removes only the top layer and reveals the colour you hid there earlier. You are drawing by taking away instead of adding.
items.twist: Plan which colour goes where in the first layer so your fireworks come out red and your stars come out yellow. That takes real forward thinking.

items.title: Salt and Watercolour Galaxy
stuff: Watery paint or ink in dark blues and purples
steps: Wet the whole paper with clean water using the brush.
Drop runny dark paint onto the wet paper and let the colours run into each other. Do not over-brush.
While it is still very wet, sprinkle salt over the whole thing.
Do not touch it. Wait until it is completely dry — this takes patience.
Brush the dry salt off and see the starburst texture underneath.
items.why: Each salt grain sucks water towards itself, dragging the colour with it and leaving a pale spot in the middle with a dark ring around it. Every grain makes its own tiny star. This is capillary action — the same force that pulls water up a plant stem.
items.twist: Try fine salt on one half and coarse salt on the other. The texture is completely different. Then flick white paint on with a toothbrush for extra stars.

items.title: Dot Drawing With a Biro
steps: Draw the outline of your object very lightly in pencil.
Now put the pencil away. From here on, no lines — only dots.
Dark areas get lots of dots very close together. Light areas get few dots, far apart. The brightest areas get no dots at all.
Build it up slowly, going over the dark areas again and again.
Stand back and look at it from across the room. The dots disappear and a picture appears.
items.why: From far away your eye cannot separate individual dots, so it averages them into grey. Lots of dots reads as dark, few dots as light. This is called stippling, and it is exactly how newspaper photographs and your phone screen work — millions of dots your eye blends together.
items.twist: Look very closely at a newspaper photograph, ideally with a magnifying glass. You will see the dots. Now you know the trick.

items.title: The 30 Circles Challenge
stuff: A bottle top to draw around
steps: Draw 30 circles on the page — 5 rows of 6 — using the bottle top as a guide.
Set a timer for 3 minutes.
Turn as many circles as you can into something real: a clock, a face, a football, a plate of ugali, a wheel, the sun, an eye, a coin.
Do not stop to think and do not judge anything. Speed matters more than quality.
When the timer stops, count how many you filled.
items.why: Most people get 8 to 12 because they slow down trying to make each one good. The exercise is about quantity beating quality — the more ideas you throw out without judging, the better ideas you reach. Designers at big companies use this exact test.
items.twist: Do it again tomorrow and the next day. Your score climbs fast. Also try: how many can you make that are NOT round objects in real life?

items.title: Draw Kitenge Patterns
stuff: A real kitenge, kanga or kikoi to look at
steps: Look at a real kitenge or kanga closely. Find one small piece of the pattern that repeats.
Divide your paper into 9 boxes with the ruler.
Fill each box with a different repeating pattern: dots, waves, triangles, spirals, leaves, zigzags.
Keep each pattern strictly inside its box. Slow, steady, no rushing.
When all 9 are full, go back and fill some boxes solid black to make the page balance.
items.why: A pattern is a rule repeated. Once you find the rule, you can fill any space with it forever. Kanga and kitenge designers work this way, and so do tile makers, wallpaper designers and mathematicians who study something called tessellation.
items.twist: Design your own kanga, including a saying along the bottom edge like real kangas have. Write it in Kiswahili.

items.title: The Road That Disappears
steps: Draw a horizontal line across the middle of the paper. That is the horizon.
Put a dot on that line. That is the vanishing point.
Draw two lines from the bottom corners of the paper up to the dot. That is your road.
Now draw electricity poles beside the road: the first one tall, and each one after it shorter, with the tops all pointing towards the dot. Space them closer together as they get nearer the dot.
Add buildings, trees and people the same way — everything shrinks towards the dot. Colour it in.
items.why: Things do not really get smaller in the distance, they just take up less of your view. Every set of parallel lines heading away from you appears to meet at one point on the horizon. Artists worked this out around 600 years ago and it changed painting forever.
items.twist: Stand at the end of a real road and hold your drawing up next to it. Then draw your own street using the same method.

items.title: Six Panel Comic of Your Day
stuff: A pencil and a black pen
steps: Rule the paper into 6 equal boxes, 2 across and 3 down.
Think of one real thing that happened today with a beginning, a middle and an end.
Plan it in pencil: box 1 sets it up, boxes 2 to 4 build it, box 5 is the biggest moment, box 6 is the ending or the joke.
Change how close you are in each box: one far away showing everything, one close on a face, one on just a hand or an object.
Ink over the pencil, add speech bubbles, rub out the pencil and colour it.
items.why: Comics work through something called closure — you draw two moments and the reader's brain invents everything that happened in between. That gap is where the reader does half the work, which is why comics feel so alive. Changing how close the view is controls how the reader feels.
items.twist: Do one every day for a week and staple them into a book. That is a real comic, made by you.

items.title: Potato Stamp Printing
stuff: A knife (adult) and a spoon handle or a blunt pencil
steps: Ask an adult to cut the potato in half cleanly.
Blot the cut face dry with a tissue — wet potato will not hold paint.
Draw a simple shape on the flat face with a pencil: a star, a leaf, a heart, your initial. Remember letters must be drawn BACKWARDS.
Ask an adult to cut away everything around your shape so it stands raised by about half a centimetre.
Press the shape into the paint, blot once on scrap paper, then stamp. Repeat in a pattern across the whole sheet.
items.why: Only the raised part touches the paper, so the shape prints and the cut-away parts do not. This is relief printing, the oldest kind of printing there is, and it is why letters have to be carved backwards to come out forwards.
items.care: The adult does all the cutting.
items.twist: Make 3 different stamps and print in a repeating sequence — star, leaf, star, leaf. Print onto an old plain t-shirt or a cloth bag with fabric paint.

items.title: One Mango, Four Ways
stuff: A mango, an orange, or any single fruit
A pencil, a black pen, colours, and charcoal
steps: Put the mango on the table and look at it for a full minute before drawing anything.
Box 1: draw it with outline only. One clean line, no shading.
Box 2: draw it in charcoal shading only, no outline at all — just light and dark.
Box 3: draw it in full colour, as realistically as you can.
Box 4: draw it as a cartoon with a face and a personality.
items.why: There is no single correct way to draw an object. An outline shows its shape, shading shows its form, colour shows its surface, and a cartoon shows an idea about it. Real artists choose which one suits what they want to say.
items.twist: Show all four to someone and ask which one feels most like the real mango. Their answer is usually not the realistic one, and that is interesting.

items.title: Draw With Your Wrong Hand
steps: Draw a simple object with your normal hand. Look at it.
Now do exactly the same drawing with your other hand.
Do not laugh and give up after ten seconds. Finish it properly.
Do 4 more drawings with the wrong hand, going slower each time.
Line all of them up in order and look at the change from the first to the last.
items.why: Your writing hand has practised for years and works on autopilot. Your other hand has not, so your brain has to think about every single movement. It feels bad, but slow deliberate movement often produces more honest, more interesting lines. Many artists do this on purpose to break their habits.
items.twist: Try drawing with a pen held in your fist, or taped to a long stick. Awkward tools force fresh results.

items.title: Draw the Same Thing 10 Days Running
stuff: A notebook, one page per day
One object you will not lose — your own left hand works perfectly
steps: Pick your subject on day 1. Your hand, your shoe, the same tree outside, or your face in a mirror.
Draw it for 15 minutes. Date the page.
Do not look back at yesterday's drawing before you start today's.
Repeat every day for 10 days without missing one.
On day 10, lay all ten out in a row.
items.why: Improvement in drawing does not come from talent, it comes from repetitions. One drawing teaches you almost nothing. Ten drawings of the same thing teach you where you keep making the same mistake, and that is exactly the thing you then fix.
items.twist: Do a second run of 10 days with a different subject and compare how much faster you improve the second time.

items.title: Balloon Rocket Run
stuff: 4 m of kamba or strong thread
A drinking straw, or a tube rolled from paper and taped
A door handle and a chair to tie to
steps: Thread the kamba through the straw, then tie one end to a door handle and the other to a chair, and pull the line tight.
Blow the balloon up big and pinch the neck shut. Do not tie it.
Tape the balloon to the straw with the neck pointing back towards the chair.
Let go and watch it fly the whole length of the line.
items.why: Air rushing out of the back pushes the balloon forward exactly as hard as the balloon pushes that air out. Every push has an equal push the other way. A real rocket does the same thing, only it pushes out burning gas instead of air.
items.twist: Set up two lines side by side and race a long thin balloon against a round one.
items.film: Put the camera at the chair end so the balloon flies straight at it.

items.title: Bottle Top Balloon Car
stuff: 2 thin sticks or skewers that slide inside a straw
steps: Ask an adult to make a hole in the middle of each bottle top with the nail. Those are your four wheels.
Tape two straws across the bottle, one near the front and one near the back.
Push a stick through each straw and press a bottle top firmly onto both ends.
Tape the balloon neck around the end of the third straw, tape that straw on top pointing backwards, blow through it, pinch it, then let go.
items.why: The stretched balloon squeezes the air inside it. Let go and that air shoots backwards out of the straw, which shoves the car forwards. The sticks spin inside the straws instead of rubbing on the bottle, so hardly any of the push is wasted as friction.
items.care: An adult makes the holes in the bottle tops.
items.twist: Blow the balloon up a bit more each run and mark how far the car goes. Turn your marks into a bar chart.
items.film: Lie the camera on the floor at wheel height for the launch.

items.title: Straw Rocket Launcher
stuff: A strip of paper about 8 cm square
A drinking straw, or a tight tube rolled from paper
A cardboard box as a target
steps: Roll the paper tightly around the pencil into a tube, tape the seam, then slide the pencil out.
Pinch one end shut and tape it. That is the nose. Cut two small paper fins and tape them at the open end.
Slide the rocket over the straw, point it high and into open space, and blow hard.
Move the target back a step at a time until you start missing.
items.why: Blowing forces air into the closed tube. The air cannot get past the sealed nose, so it presses on the inside of the nose and shoves the rocket off the straw. The fins drag at the back, which keeps the heavy nose pointing forward instead of tumbling.
items.care: Never point it at a face, an animal, a window or anyone standing nearby. Aim high and into open space.
items.twist: Build one rocket with fins and one without, and see which flies straighter.
items.film: Film in slow motion right at the moment it leaves the straw.

items.title: Matchbox Catapult
stuff: A flat stick or a lolly stick
Squashed paper balls to fire, and bottle tops as targets
steps: Band the stick flat along the top of the matchbox so it sticks out past one end.
Band the spoon to the stick with the bowl facing up and hanging over the edge.
Stand the bottle tops up on the floor as targets.
Load a paper ball, hold the matchbox down, pull the spoon back and let go.
items.why: Pulling the spoon back bends it and stretches the rubber, and stretched rubber stores energy. Let go and all that stored energy turns into movement in a fraction of a second, which is far faster than your hand could ever throw it.
items.care: Fire at floor targets or a wall only. Never at people, animals or windows. Paper balls only, never stones.
items.twist: Pull the spoon back the same amount every time and change only the number of rubber bands. Measure each distance.
items.film: Camera low behind the targets so they fly at the lens.

items.title: Gazeti Glider Test
stuff: A ruler, or a piece of kamba you mark and measure afterwards
steps: Fold one glider as a sharp dart, one with long wide wings, and one short and fat.
Chalk a throwing line on the floor.
Throw each one three times from that line and chalk where it lands.
Tape a bottle top to the nose of the worst flyer and throw it again.
items.why: A wing flies by bending air downwards as it slides through it, and the air pushes back up. That upward push is lift. Long wings make more lift but drag more, so they fly slowly and far. Nose weight stops the plane stalling because it keeps the nose tipped slightly down into the air.
items.twist: Test them outside on a windy day and again in a still room. One design copes far better.
items.film: Throw from behind the camera so all three flights are in one shot.

items.title: Hoop Glider
stuff: A drinking straw, or a tight tube rolled from paper
steps: Cut two paper strips, one about 2 cm wide and one about 4 cm wide.
Tape each strip into a loop, making one small hoop and one big hoop.
Tape the small hoop to one end of the straw and the big hoop to the other.
Hold it with the small hoop in front and throw it gently, like a spear.
items.why: It looks wrong, but each hoop is just a wing bent into a circle, so it makes lift whichever way it rolls. The big hoop drags more than the small one, and that difference keeps the nose pointing forward instead of tumbling end over end.
items.twist: Slide the hoops closer together, then further apart. One spacing glides much further than the rest.
items.film: Walk backwards filming while someone throws it towards you.

items.title: Paper Whirlybird
stuff: A paper strip about 20 cm by 5 cm
A chair or a step to drop from
steps: Cut a slit halfway down the middle from the top, and fold the two flaps out in opposite directions. Those are the blades.
Fold the bottom third up and hold it with the paper clip.
Ask an adult to hold the chair, stand on it and drop the whirlybird.
Cut the blades shorter and drop it again.
items.why: Rising air hits the two blades at opposite angles, so one blade is pushed one way and the other the opposite way. That pair of pushes twists it into a spin, and spinning drags hard on the air so it falls slowly. Real sycamore seeds fall in exactly this way.
items.care: An adult holds the chair while you stand on it.
items.twist: Add a second paper clip. Does heavier mean faster spinning, or just faster falling? Time it and see.
items.film: Film from below looking up as it comes down.

items.title: Newspaper Kite
stuff: 2 thin straight sticks, or straws taped end to end
A strip of plastic bag for the tail
steps: Tape the sticks into a cross, with the short one about a third of the way down the long one.
Lay the cross on the newspaper, cut round it leaving 2 cm spare, and fold the edges over the sticks and tape them down.
Tie a loose loop of kamba from the top of the long stick to the bottom, then tie your flying line to the middle of that loop.
Tape a plastic tail about a metre long to the bottom, then run into the wind.
items.why: The kite sits at an angle to the wind, so moving air is pushed downwards off its face and the air shoves the kite up and back. The line stops it escaping, and the tail drags behind so the kite cannot spin round and dive.
items.care: Never fly a kite near power lines, roads or rooftops.
items.twist: Cut the tail shorter bit by bit until it starts spinning. Now you know the shortest tail that works.
items.film: One shot looking straight up the line to the kite.

items.title: Plastic Bag Parachute
stuff: A bottle top as the load
steps: Cut a square from the bag about 30 cm across.
Tape a thread to each corner.
Tie all four threads to the bottle top so it hangs level.
Drop it from as high as you can safely reach and time the fall, then cut a small hole in the middle and drop it again.
items.why: The open canopy has to shove a lot of air out of the way, and air resistance grows as the canopy grows, so a big one falls slowly. A hole in the middle lets trapped air escape steadily instead of spilling out of one side, which is what stops it rocking.
items.twist: Race a 30 cm canopy against a 15 cm one, dropped at exactly the same moment.
items.film: Drop it past the camera from above and film the landing.

items.title: Soap Powered Boat
stuff: A flat piece of plastic cut from a bottle or a lid
A karai or basin of clean water
steps: Cut a boat shape about 5 cm long with a small notch cut into the back end.
Float it gently on still water without putting your fingers in.
Dip the matchstick in the soap and touch it into the notch at the back.
Watch the boat shoot across the basin.
items.why: Water molecules pull on each other, and at the surface that pull behaves like a stretched skin. Soap breaks the pull wherever it lands, so the water in front of the boat is still pulling hard while the water behind it is not, and the boat gets dragged forwards.
items.care: Change the water for a clean lot before every run.
items.twist: It only works once per basin. Count how many runs you get before it stops working, and you will know when the soap has spread everywhere.
items.film: Film from directly above the basin so the dash across is obvious.

items.title: Rubber Band Paddle Boat
stuff: An empty plastic bottle or a flat piece of wood
A rectangle of stiff plastic for the paddle
A basin or bath of water
steps: Tape a stick along each side of the bottle so both stick out about 6 cm past the back.
Loop a rubber band between the two sticks so it stretches across the gap.
Slide the plastic paddle into the loop, then wind the paddle over and over to twist the band.
Hold the paddle still, put the boat in the water, and let go.
items.why: Twisting the rubber band stores energy in the stretched rubber. As it unwinds it spins the paddle, and the paddle shoves water backwards. Pushing water back means the water pushes the boat forward by exactly the same amount.
items.twist: Count your winds. Twenty, then forty, then sixty. Does twice the winding really give twice the distance?
items.film: Start filming before you let go so the wind-up is in the shot.

items.title: Bottle Top Hovercraft
stuff: A flat round lid — a margarine tub lid, or an old CD
A nail (adult) and a smooth table
steps: Ask an adult to make a hole the size of a pen tip in the middle of the bottle top, and a matching hole in the middle of the lid.
Glue or tape the bottle top over the hole in the lid, sealing all the way round so air can only leave through the holes.
Blow the balloon up big and pinch the neck.
Stretch the balloon over the bottle top without letting the air out, then let go and give the lid a small push.
items.why: Escaping air is trapped between the lid and the table, so it lifts the lid onto a cushion of air a fraction of a millimetre thick. With almost nothing touching the table there is almost no friction, so one small push keeps it sliding for ages.
items.twist: Try it on a table, then on a floor, then on a carpet. Air cushions hate rough surfaces. Find out how rough is too rough.
items.film: Film at table height so it looks like it is floating.
items.care: An adult makes the holes.

items.title: Zip Line Rider
stuff: 5 m of kamba or strong thread
A matchbox or small tin as cargo
A toy figure if you have one
steps: Cut a 4 cm piece of straw and thread the kamba through it first, before you tie anything.
Tie the top end high, to a window latch or a branch, and the bottom end to a chair leg, then pull it tight.
Tape the cargo under the straw.
Hold it at the top, let go, and time the run. Then move the chair to change the steepness and time it again.
items.why: Gravity pulls the cargo straight down, but the line will only let it move along the slope, so down the slope is where it goes. The steeper the line, the bigger the share of gravity that points along it, and the faster the ride.
items.twist: Tape a paper flap on as a brake and find the smallest slope that still gets it all the way down.
items.film: Tape the phone to the cargo for a rider's-eye run, if it is a short drop over something soft.

items.title: The Come Back Tin
stuff: A round tin or plastic tub with a lid
A heavy nut, bolt or a stone with a hole in it
steps: Ask an adult to make a small hole in the centre of the base and the centre of the lid.
Thread the rubber band through both holes and hold it at each end with a matchstick pushed through the loop.
Hang the weight from the middle of the rubber band inside, then press the lid on.
Roll the tin gently away from you across the floor and wait.
items.why: As the tin rolls, both ends of the rubber band turn with it, but the weight is too heavy to swing up so it stays at the bottom. That means the band winds tighter and tighter, storing the energy of your roll. When the tin stops, the band unwinds and rolls it straight back to you.
items.care: An adult makes the holes. Tape over any sharp tin edge.
items.twist: Roll it harder and harder. Try to find the roll that is too strong for it to come back.
items.film: Roll it away from a low camera so it disappears and then returns.

items.title: Bottle Top Spinner
stuff: A matchstick or a short stick
steps: Ask an adult to make a hole in the centre of each bottle top.
Push the stick through both tops so they sit back to back with the stick poking out below.
Stick a paper disc on top and colour it in segments or a spiral.
Spin it hard on a smooth floor and time how long it lasts.
items.why: Once something is spinning it keeps spinning until something takes the spin away, and here that something is friction with the floor and the air. Keeping the weight out at the rim makes the spin much harder to slow, which is why two tops beat one.
items.care: An adult makes the holes.
items.twist: Colour half the disc red and half blue, spin it fast, and see what colour your eyes report back.
items.film: Film from straight above so the pattern blurs into one colour.

items.title: Buzzing Button
stuff: A big button with two holes, or a bottle top
A nail (adult) if you are using a bottle top
steps: If you are using a bottle top, ask an adult to make two holes near the middle.
Thread the string through one hole and back through the other, then tie the two ends into one big loop.
Slide the button to the middle, hook a finger in each end, and swing the button over and over to wind the string up.
Pull your hands apart, let them come back in, and repeat until it hums.
items.why: Winding stores twist in the string. When you pull, that twist has to unwind, so the button spins fast, and its spin carries on far enough to wind the string the other way ready for your next pull. The hum is the button chopping the air fast enough for your ears to hear it as a note.
items.care: An adult makes the holes. Keep it well away from your face and your hair.
items.twist: Cut small notches round the edge of the top and listen to how the sound changes.
items.film: Get the microphone close so the hum is loud on the recording.

items.title: Katoni Air Cannon
stuff: A cardboard box or a bucket
Paper cups or bottle tops as targets
steps: Tape the box shut and cut a round hole about 10 cm across in the middle of one side.
Cut the opposite side out, stretch the plastic bag over the opening and tape it down tight all the way round.
Stand the cups in a line two metres away.
Aim the hole at the cups and thump the plastic sharply with your palm.
items.why: The thump shoves a lump of air out of the hole all at once. Air at the rim of the hole drags on that lump and rolls it into a spinning doughnut, and a spinning ring holds itself together instead of spreading out. That is how it can cross a room and still knock a cup over.
items.care: Aim at targets only, never at anyone's face or ears.
items.twist: Cut a bigger hole in a second box and see which one knocks cups over from further away.
items.film: Camera beside the cups, and thump on a count of three.

items.title: Tin Stilts
stuff: 2 strong empty tins the same size
steps: Ask an adult to punch two holes opposite each other near the closed end of each tin, and to tape over any sharp edge.
Thread kamba through both holes of one tin and tie a loop long enough to reach your hand when you stand on it. Do the same with the other.
Stand on the tins with the closed ends down, pull both ropes tight, and take your first steps on grass.
Once you can walk, set out a course and time yourself round it.
items.why: Standing on tins lifts your centre of gravity, which is the balance point of your whole body. The higher it is, the faster you tip, so you have to keep shuffling to stay underneath it. Pulling the ropes tight presses the tins against your feet so friction holds them on.
items.care: An adult makes the holes and tapes every sharp edge. Walk on soft ground, never near stairs, water or a road.
items.twist: Try a taller pair of tins. There is a height where balancing becomes almost impossible. Find it.
items.film: Film your feet for the first wobble, then step back for the walk.

items.title: Magnet Racer
stuff: A magnet from a broken speaker, or a fridge magnet
A sheet of stiff paper or card
2 tins or books to lift the paper
steps: Draw a race track on the paper.
Rest the paper across two tins so there is a gap underneath.
Put the paper clip on the track and hold the magnet under the paper, right below it.
Move the magnet and steer the clip round the track without touching it.
items.why: A magnet pulls on iron and steel from a distance, and paper does nothing at all to block that pull. The clip is not being pushed by the paper. It is being pulled through the paper by the magnet underneath.
items.twist: Slide a second sheet under the clip, then a third. Count how many sheets it takes before the magnet loses its grip.
items.film: Film from above so it looks like the clip is moving on its own.

items.title: The Fizz Rocket
stuff: A small plastic bottle, never glass
A cork or a tightly rolled paper plug that fits the neck
A square of tissue, an adult, and open ground
