steps: Go outside onto open ground with an adult. Everyone stands well back before you start.
Wrap the baking soda in the tissue to make a small parcel that fits through the neck.
Pour the siki into the bottle, drop the parcel in, push the cork in firmly, and stand the bottle upside down on the ground pointing straight up.
Walk five big steps away at once and wait. If nothing happens in two minutes, leave it and let the adult open it.
items.why: Baking soda and siki react and make carbon dioxide gas. That gas takes up far more room than the liquid it came from, so pressure inside climbs until it is strong enough to shove the cork out. The same push that fires the cork down fires the bottle up.
items.care: Outside only, with an adult, pointing straight up on open ground. Never lean over it, never aim it at a person, an animal, a window or a roof, and never use a glass bottle.
items.twist: Try more siki, then less, and find the mix that launches highest. Keep everybody the same distance back every single time.
items.film: Set the phone on the ground a good distance away and let it record the whole wait.

items.title: Ramp Race
stuff: A long piece of stiff cardboard
A bottle top or a small ball
Chalk or tape to mark the floor
A ruler, or a piece of kamba you mark and measure afterwards
steps: Lean the cardboard on one book to make a gentle ramp, and mark the floor at the bottom of it.
Let the bottle top roll from the very top without pushing it, and mark where it stops.
Add a book, then another, then another, marking every run.
Line all your marks up and look at how the distance grows.
items.why: Lifting the bottle top higher gives it more stored height energy, and rolling down turns all of it into speed. More speed at the bottom means friction has to work for longer to stop it, so it goes further. It will not go twice as far for twice the height though, because friction is stubborn.
items.twist: Run the whole test again on carpet. The shape of the pattern changes, not just the numbers.
items.film: Film along the floor so all the chalk marks are in one line.

items.title: Volcano Race
stuff: A tray or karai, dish soap, and beetroot juice or manjano for colour
steps: Stand both bottles in the tray and put two spoons of baking soda in each, with a squeeze of soap and a little colour.
Give one person the siki and the other the ndimu juice.
Pour both in at the same moment and watch which foam climbs higher.
Mark the winning height on the bottle with a strip of tape.
items.why: Siki and ndimu juice are both acids, and both react with baking soda to make carbon dioxide gas. The soap traps that gas as foam so you can see it. Shop vinegar is usually the stronger acid, so it makes gas faster than the foam can collapse and wins.
items.care: Keep it away from your eyes. Siki stings.
items.twist: Leave one lot of siki in the sun for an hour and race warm siki against cold.
items.film: Two bottles in frame, count down from three, pour together.

items.title: Fizz Bag Pop
stuff: A zip bag, or a strong plastic bag and a tie
steps: Go outside. Pour the siki into the bag.
Wrap the baking soda in the tissue and twist it shut.
Drop the parcel in, seal the bag fast, shake it once, and put it on the ground.
Stand well back and wait for the bang.
items.why: The tissue buys you a few seconds before the baking soda meets the acid. Then carbon dioxide pours out, and the gas needs far more room than the bag has, so pressure builds until the weakest seam gives way with a bang.
items.care: Outside only, on the ground, standing back. Never hold it, and never use a glass jar or a bottle with a screw lid.
items.twist: Halve the baking soda and try again. Is there an amount too small to pop the bag?
items.film: Put the camera down at bag height and step away before it goes.

items.title: Manjano Colour Switch
stuff: Half a cup of warm water
Baking soda mixed into a little water
Ndimu juice and a brush or cotton bud
steps: Stir the manjano into the warm water, let it settle, then paint the yellow liquid onto the paper strips and let them dry.
Paint a line of baking soda water across a dry strip and watch it turn red.
Now paint ndimu juice over the red line.
The red should swing back to yellow.
items.why: Manjano contains a colour called curcumin that changes shape when it meets an alkali such as baking soda, and the new shape looks red. An acid like ndimu juice pushes it back to its yellow shape. Scientists use exactly this trick, with other dyes, to test whether something is acid or alkali.
items.care: Nothing goes in your mouth. Manjano stains clothes and worktops, so work on newspaper.
items.twist: Test soap water, sugar water, tea and toothpaste on your strips and sort the house into acids and alkalis.
items.film: Hold the strip still and paint slowly, in close-up. The colour change is the whole shot.

items.title: Invisible Ink
stuff: A cotton bud or a stick with cotton on the end
A warm iron or a candle (adult)
steps: Squeeze the ndimu juice into a cup and add a few drops of water.
Write your message with the cotton bud and let the paper dry completely until it vanishes.
Ask an adult to run a warm iron over the paper, or to hold it near a candle for you.
Read the brown message as it appears.
items.why: Ndimu juice soaks into the paper fibres and dries clear. The sugars and acids in it break down and go brown at a lower temperature than paper does, so gentle heat browns your writing while the rest of the page stays white.
items.care: An adult does all the heating. Never hold paper near a flame yourself.
items.twist: Try milk and onion juice as well and see which one comes out clearest.
items.film: Fix the camera on the blank page and let the writing appear in one unbroken shot.

items.title: Magic Milk
stuff: Enough milk to cover the bottom
4 different colours — ink from a pen, beetroot juice, strong black tea, manjano paste
steps: Pour milk into the plate about half a centimetre deep and let it settle completely still.
Drop the colours in four separate spots near the middle.
Dip the tip of the cotton bud into the dish soap.
Touch it into the middle of one colour and hold it there without stirring.
items.why: Milk is water with tiny drops of fat floating in it, and its surface is held tight by water pulling on itself. Soap grabs the fat and breaks that tight surface where it touches, so the surface rushes away from the soap and drags the colours with it. It keeps moving until the soap has found all the fat.
items.care: Nothing goes in your mouth. Pour it away afterwards.
items.twist: Do it again with water instead of milk. Almost nothing happens, and that is your proof the fat matters.
items.film: Straight down from above, close, and do not move the camera when you touch the soap in.

items.title: Bubble Lava Lamp
stuff: A clear bottle or tall glass
Cooking oil to fill it two thirds
Water coloured with beetroot juice, manjano or ink from a pen
steps: Put the baking soda in the bottom of the bottle, then pour the oil in on top.
Pour the coloured water in slowly. It sinks straight through the oil.
Pour a splash of siki in and watch coloured blobs climb.
Add more siki whenever it slows down.
items.why: Oil floats because it is less dense than water, meaning the same amount of it weighs less. When the siki reaches the baking soda at the bottom it makes carbon dioxide bubbles, and each bubble carries a blob of coloured water up with it. At the top the bubble escapes and the heavier water sinks back down.
items.care: Nothing goes in your mouth. Do it on a tray.
items.twist: Turn the lights off and shine a torch through the back of the bottle.
items.film: Dark room, torch behind, camera in front. It looks like a real lava lamp.

items.title: Oobleck
stuff: 2 cups of corn starch (the Maizena packet at the duka). Plain unga wa ugali will not work
Beetroot juice or manjano for colour, if you want it
steps: Put the cornflour in the bowl and add the water slowly, mixing with your hand.
Stop adding water when it pours like a liquid but goes hard the instant you tap it.
Punch it fast, then let a finger sink in slowly, and feel the difference.
Roll a ball between your palms, then stop moving and watch it melt away.
items.why: It is millions of tiny grains floating in water. Hit it fast and the grains have no time to slide past each other, so they jam together and behave like a solid. Move slowly and water has time to flow between the grains, so it behaves like a liquid.
items.care: Never pour it down the sink. It sets hard in the pipe. Bin it or put it on the garden.
items.twist: Spread it on a tin and hum loudly against the tin. The vibration makes it dance.
items.film: Slow motion of the punch, then real speed of your finger sinking in.

items.title: The Rubber Egg
stuff: Enough siki to cover the egg
steps: Put the egg in the glass and pour siki over until it is completely covered.
Watch the bubbles start straight away, then leave it somewhere safe.
Change the siki for fresh siki after the first day.
On day two lift it out, rinse it gently, and bounce it from 5 cm above a plate.
items.why: An eggshell is made of calcium carbonate, and the acid in siki reacts with it and turns it into gas and dissolved calcium. The bubbles are carbon dioxide leaving the shell. Once the shell has gone, only the rubbery skin underneath is left, and that skin stretches.
items.care: Bounce it low and over a plate. It will burst in the end, and it is raw egg, so wash your hands afterwards.
items.twist: Shine a torch through it in a dark room. You can see the yolk floating inside.
items.film: Day one and day two side by side, then one slow motion bounce.

items.title: The Invisible Fire Blanket
steps: Stand the candle on the tray and ask an adult to light it and stay with you.
Put the baking soda in the glass and pour the siki on.
Wait for the fizzing to slow down, then tip the glass slowly over the candle as if pouring, but let no liquid fall out.
The flame goes out with nothing you can see touching it.
items.why: The reaction fills the glass with carbon dioxide, a gas about half again as heavy as air, so it sits in the glass and can be poured. It washes over the candle and pushes the oxygen away, and without oxygen a flame cannot keep burning.
items.care: An adult lights the candle and stays for the whole thing. Roll your sleeves back and keep paper well away.
items.twist: Pour plain air from an empty glass first, so you have proved it is the gas doing the work.
items.film: Close on the flame, and keep the glass in shot so people can see no liquid falls.

items.title: Balloon Blower
stuff: A funnel or a rolled paper cone
steps: Pour the siki into the bottle.
Use the funnel to get the baking soda inside the balloon.
Stretch the balloon over the neck of the bottle, keeping the powder up inside the balloon.
Lift the balloon upright so the powder drops in, and watch it blow itself up.
items.why: The acid and the baking soda swap parts, and one of the things they make is carbon dioxide gas. The gas cannot get past the balloon so it fills it. A spoonful of powder makes a surprising amount of gas, because a gas is mostly empty space between its molecules.
items.care: Plastic bottle only, and nothing on the top except the balloon.
items.twist: Use the same bottle and balloon each time and mark the balloon size for 1, 2 and 3 spoons of baking soda.
items.film: Fix the camera on the bottle and let the balloon rise in one shot.

items.title: Salt Crystal Rock
stuff: A cup of very hot water (adult pours it)
steps: Ask an adult to pour the hot water into the jar.
Stir in chumvi a spoon at a time until no more will dissolve and grains sit on the bottom.
Tie the thread to the pencil, rest the pencil across the jar so the thread hangs in the water, and put it somewhere it will not be knocked.
Look at it every day for a week without moving it.
items.why: Hot water holds far more dissolved salt than cold water. As the jar cools and the water slowly evaporates there is more salt than the water can hold, so the extra locks onto your thread. Salt always builds the same cube shape, because of the way its particles stack.
items.care: An adult handles the hot water.
items.twist: Grow a second jar with sugar instead and compare the two crystal shapes closely.
items.film: One photo a day at the same angle, then cut them together into a five second time lapse.

items.title: Colour Chase
stuff: Strips of white paper — a paper napkin works best, an exercise book page works slower
Felt tip pens, especially black ones
steps: Draw a fat dot of pen about 2 cm up from the end of each strip.
Tape the top of each strip to the pencil and rest the pencil across the saucer.
Set the height so the very bottom of the paper is in the water but the dot stays above it.
Wait five minutes and watch the colours climb and separate.
items.why: Water creeps up the paper because it clings to the fibres and to itself. Ink is a mixture of different coloured chemicals, and each one sticks to the paper by a different amount. The ones that cling least get carried furthest, so the mixture splits into stripes.
items.twist: Test five different black pens. No two brands build black out of the same mix.
items.film: Time lapse of the colours climbing, then hold the finished strips up together.

items.title: Ice Lift
steps: Float the ice cube in the glass.
Lay the thread across the top of the cube.
Sprinkle chumvi along the thread where it touches the ice.
Count slowly to twenty, then lift the thread and the cube comes up with it.
items.why: Salt makes ice melt at a temperature below zero, so the salty patch melts. That melting pulls heat out of the water around it, the salt then spreads out and gets weaker, and the water refreezes, this time around your thread.
items.twist: Try sugar instead of salt. It works far worse, which tells you it is not simply about being a powder.
items.film: Close up on the lift, with no cuts, so nobody can accuse you of cheating.

items.title: Climbing Water
stuff: Beetroot juice, manjano, or ink from a pen
2 strips of old cotton cloth, or 2 paper napkins
steps: Fill the two outer glasses with coloured water and leave the middle one empty.
Fold each paper strip into a thick rope.
Hang one end of each rope in a full glass and the other end in the empty middle glass.
Come back in an hour, and again the next morning.
items.why: Water molecules cling to the paper fibres and pull each other along behind, so water climbs the paper against gravity. That is capillary action. It carries on until all three glasses sit at the same level, because after that gravity pulls back exactly as hard as the paper pulls.
items.twist: Put yellow in one end glass and blue in the other, and see what colour arrives in the middle.
items.film: Same angle, one photo every fifteen minutes, then run them fast.

items.title: Density Tower
stuff: A tall clear glass or bottle
Honey, or thick syrup made by stirring 4 spoons of sugar into 1 spoon of hot water (adult)
A small stone, a bottle top and a dry bean
steps: Pour honey into the bottom without letting it touch the sides.
Pour the coloured water slowly down the inside of the glass on top of it.
Pour the oil on last, just as slowly.
Drop the stone, the bottle top and the bean in one at a time and see where each one stops.
items.why: Density is how much a thing weighs for its size. Honey is heaviest for its size so it sits at the bottom, then water, then oil on top. Each object sinks until it meets a layer that is heavier for its size than it is, and that is where it floats.
items.care: Nothing in the glass goes in your mouth.
items.twist: Try adding a layer of soapy water between the honey and the water and see whether it stays put.
items.film: Pour in close-up, then pull back for the three objects landing at three different heights.

items.title: Egg in the Bottle
stuff: A hard boiled egg with the shell off
A glass bottle with a mouth just smaller than the egg
steps: Ask an adult to hard boil the egg, then peel it once it is cool.
Rub a little oil round the mouth of the bottle.
Ask the adult to light the paper strip and drop it into the bottle.
Sit the egg on the mouth straight away and watch it get sucked in.
items.why: The burning paper heats the air in the bottle, and hot air spreads out, so some of it escapes past the egg. When the flame dies the air left inside cools and shrinks, so there is less air pushing out than the air outside is pushing in, and the outside air shoves the egg through the neck.
items.care: The adult lights the paper and handles the bottle. Keep your face away from the mouth of the bottle.
items.twist: To get it out again, tip the bottle so the egg blocks the neck, blow hard into it, then stand back.
items.film: Side on, so the moment it squeezes through the neck is clear.

items.title: Milk Plastic
stuff: 4 spoons of siki, or the juice of 2 ndimu
A sieve or a clean cloth
steps: Ask an adult to heat the milk until it steams, but not until it boils, then take it off the heat.
Stir the siki in slowly. Lumps appear within seconds.
Once the adult has poured it out, strain the lumps through the cloth and squeeze the water out.
Squash the lumps into a shape and leave it to dry hard for two days.
items.why: Milk carries a protein called casein, whose long molecules normally drift apart from each other. Acid makes them clump and tangle into one solid mass, and once it dries that tangle is stiff and hard. Buttons really were made this way a hundred years ago.
items.care: The adult does the heating and the pouring. Hot milk burns.
items.twist: Press a coin into it while it is still soft to make a medal, or colour it with beetroot juice.
items.film: Film the lumps appearing, then a second clip two days later of the hard finished piece.

items.title: Dancing Beans
stuff: A handful of maharagwe or dry rice
steps: Fill the glass with fizzy soda and wait for the first big froth to settle.
Drop in five or six dry beans.
Watch them sink, collect bubbles, rise, and drop again.
Shine the torch through the glass to see it properly.
items.why: The soda is packed with dissolved carbon dioxide, and bubbles form on the rough skin of each bean. Enough bubbles make the bean and its bubbles together lighter for their size than the drink, so up it goes. At the surface the bubbles burst, the bean is heavy again, and it sinks.
items.care: This one is an experiment, not a drink. Pour it away afterwards.
items.twist: Race a raisin, a grain of rice and a small bottle top. Which one dances longest, and why?
items.film: Torch behind the glass, camera in front, and let it run for a full minute.

items.title: Newspaper Tower Challenge
stuff: A tin as the test weight
A ruler, or a piece of kamba you mark and measure afterwards
steps: Roll each sheet tightly from one corner into a long thin tube and tape it.
Build the tallest tower you can that stands on its own, using triangles rather than squares.
Measure it.
Balance the tin on top and see whether it holds.
items.why: A rolled tube is far stronger than a flat sheet, because paper on the outside of the curve has to stretch before the tube can bend, and paper hates stretching. Triangles cannot change shape unless a side changes length, so a triangle frame stays rigid while a square frame folds flat.
items.twist: Build a second tower using only squares, load them both, and watch the difference.
items.film: Time lapse of the build, then the tin going on at real speed.

items.title: Newspaper Bridge
stuff: Tins or full bottles as the load
steps: Stand the two chairs about 40 cm apart.
Lay a flat sheet across the gap and load it until it sags. Notice how little it takes.
Fold a fresh sheet into a fan of narrow pleats and lay that across the same gap.
Load the pleated one until it fails, and compare.
items.why: Pleats make the paper deep instead of flat. When a beam bends, the top squashes and the bottom stretches, and the further apart those two faces are, the harder it is to bend at all. That is exactly why corrugated cardboard and steel girders are shaped the way they are.
items.twist: Try a tube instead of pleats. Which carries more, from the same single sheet?
items.film: Side on at bridge height, adding one tin at a time until it drops.

items.title: Straw Truss Bridge
stuff: A cup and some stones as the load
steps: Tape straws into ten triangles the same size.
Join five triangles in a row to make one flat side, do the same again, then join the two sides with straws across the top and bottom.
Rest the bridge between the two stacks of books.
Hang the cup from the middle and add stones one at a time until it fails.
items.why: A load on a truss splits into pushes and pulls that run along each straw to the supports. Straws are surprisingly strong when pushed or pulled end to end, and very weak when bent, so a good bridge is arranged so no straw is ever asked to bend.
items.twist: Rebuild it with squares instead of triangles and count how many stones you lose.
items.film: Camera on the cup. The failure is the shot.

items.title: Katoni Den
stuff: A blunt knife or scissors (adult cuts)
An old kanga or kitenge for the door
steps: Flatten the biggest box for the floor and stand the others up around it.
Mark where you want a door and a window, and ask an adult to cut them.
Tape the walls to each other from the inside, then add a folded sheet of cardboard as a sloping roof.
Hang the cloth over the door, put the torch inside and move in.
items.why: Cardboard is a sandwich: two flat sheets with a wavy layer glued between them. The wave is a row of little arches, so a squash on the surface gets carried sideways along the arch instead of crushing the board. That is how something this light holds up a roof.
items.care: An adult does all the cutting. Never build where it could fall on you, and never on stairs.
items.twist: Fold triangles of card into the corners as braces and feel how much less the walls wobble.
items.film: Walk the camera in through the door for the reveal.

items.title: Bottle Top Marble Run
stuff: A big flat piece of cardboard
Toilet roll tubes or tubes rolled from paper
A marble, a bean or a bottle top
steps: Stand the big card up against a wall.
Tape the tubes on in a zigzag, each one sloping slightly downhill into the next.
Put the tin at the bottom as the goal.
Drop the marble in the top and fix every place it escapes.
items.why: Every drop between tubes turns height into speed, and every flat run and every wall it clips takes some of that speed back as heat and sound. The run only works if each tube starts lower than the last, because the marble can never climb higher than where it started.
items.twist: Time it, then try to build the slowest run that still finishes.
items.film: Follow the marble down in one unbroken shot. It takes a few goes.

items.title: Window Pulley
stuff: A bottle top with a hole through the middle, or an empty cotton reel
A pencil or stick for the axle
steps: Push the stick through the reel so it spins freely, and tape the stick across a window frame or between two chair backs, up high.
Run the kamba over the reel so both ends hang down.
Tie the tin to one end.
Pull the other end down to lift the tin, then load the tin up and feel the difference.
items.why: A single pulley does not make the load lighter. It changes which way you pull, and pulling down is easier because you can add your own weight to it. The reel spins so the rope runs over a turning surface instead of dragging, which wastes much less of your effort.
items.twist: Hang a second pulley on the rope with the load, and the same pull lifts twice as much, but only half as far.
items.film: Send something up to a window and film it arriving from up there.

items.title: Hanger Balance Scale
stuff: A wire coat hanger or a straight stick
A door handle to hang it from
Coins or bottle tops as weights
steps: Punch three holes evenly round the rim of each cup and tie three threads to each to make a hanging basket.
Hang one basket at each end of the hanger.
Hang the hanger from a door handle so it swings free, and adjust until it hangs level when empty.
Put an object in one side and add bottle tops to the other until it balances, then write down how many tops it weighs.
items.why: The hanger tips until the turning effect on each side is the same, and turning effect is the weight multiplied by its distance from the middle. Because both baskets hang the same distance out, level means the two weights are equal. A market scale does exactly this.
items.twist: Move one basket closer to the middle. It will now lift a much heavier load, because you have built a lever.
items.film: Weigh five things and read the results out. Short, and oddly satisfying.

items.title: Bottle Water Wheel
stuff: A stick or pencil for the axle
A nail (adult) and a basin of water
steps: Ask an adult to make a hole through the centre of the bottle's base and its lid so the stick passes right through.
Tape the six tops or spoons round the side of the bottle, all facing the same way so they can catch water.
Push the stick through so the bottle spins freely on it.
Hold it under a slow stream of water, over the basin, and let it spin.
items.why: Falling water carries energy, because gravity has been pulling it down. When it lands in a cup it gets stopped, and the push of stopping it turns the wheel. A real water turbine makes electricity in exactly this way, only much bigger.
items.care: An adult makes the holes. Work outside or over a basin, and catch the water to reuse it.
items.twist: Tie a thread to the axle and see if your wheel can wind a bottle top up off the ground.
items.film: Close on the cups filling and tipping, in slow motion.

items.title: Katoni Periscope
stuff: A long thin box, or cardboard taped into a tube
2 small flat mirrors — a handbag mirror, or cheap mirror tiles from a duka
A corner of paper to check the angle
steps: Mark a window at the top of the front and another at the bottom of the back, and ask an adult to cut them.
Tape one mirror inside the top, tilted at 45 degrees, facing the top window.
Tape the second mirror inside the bottom, tilted the opposite way, facing the bottom window.
Look in the bottom window and see over a wall.
items.why: Light bounces off a mirror at the same angle it arrived. A mirror tilted at 45 degrees turns light through a right angle, so the top mirror sends the view straight down the tube and the bottom mirror turns it into your eye.
items.care: An adult does the cutting. Tape round the edges of any mirror glass.
items.twist: Take it outside and watch round a corner without being seen.
items.film: Hold the camera at the eyepiece and show what the periscope sees.

items.title: Tripwire Alarm
steps: Thread the lids onto a short string so they hang together and clatter.
Tape the stick across the top of the door frame with the lids dangling from it.
Tie a long thread to the stick and run it across the doorway at ankle height, tied loosely to a chair leg on the other side.
Tell everyone in the house it is there, then wait.
items.why: The tripwire stores nothing on its own. It simply moves the stick when someone pushes into it, and that small movement is enough to swing the lids into each other. Every collision sets the metal vibrating, which shakes the air and reaches your ears as noise.
items.care: Ankle height on a flat floor only, never on stairs and never where someone could fall. Tell everyone in the house before you set it.
items.twist: Add a second thread higher up so it catches adults as well.
items.film: Hide the camera pointing at the door and wait for a victim.

items.title: Cardboard Grabber Hand
steps: Draw round your hand on the card and cut the shape out.
Cut each straw into three short pieces and tape them along each finger, leaving a gap at each knuckle.
Thread a length of thread down through the straws of each finger and tape the end at the fingertip.
Pull all five threads at once and the hand closes.
items.why: The straws are your bones and the threads are tendons. Your real fingers contain no muscles at all. The muscles are in your palm and forearm and they pull on tendons exactly like these to curl your fingers.
items.twist: Feel the back of your own hand while you wiggle one finger. Those moving cords under the skin are the real thing.
items.film: Your real hand and the cardboard one side by side, doing the same movement.

items.title: Matchbox Secret Chest
stuff: A bead or a small bottle top for each handle
steps: Slide the trays out, glue the outer sleeves together into a block, and slide the trays back in.
Cover the whole outside with paper and decorate it.
Glue a bead or a top onto the end of each drawer as a handle.
Label the drawers and fill them with your smallest treasures.
items.why: Glue works because it flows into every dip and scratch on the cardboard and then hardens there, locking the two surfaces together. Six boxes glued face to face are far stiffer than six loose ones, because none of them can slide against its neighbour any more.
items.twist: Build a false bottom into one drawer by gluing a card in halfway down.
items.film: Open every drawer one at a time at the end, like a reveal.

items.title: Tin Can Telephone
stuff: 10 m of thin kamba or fishing line
steps: Ask an adult to punch a hole in the centre of the closed end of each tin and to tape over any sharp edge.
Thread the kamba in from the outside and tie it round a matchstick inside so it cannot pull back out. Do the same at the other end.
Walk apart until the line is tight and touching nothing.
One of you talks into a tin while the other listens with a tin at their ear.
items.why: Your voice makes the base of the tin vibrate. Those vibrations travel along the tight string as a wave, faster and with less loss than through open air, then shake the far tin's base, which pushes air into your friend's ear. A slack string just bends instead of carrying the wave, which is why it has to be tight.
items.care: An adult makes the holes and covers every sharp edge.
items.twist: Get someone to pinch the string in the middle while you talk. The call dies instantly.
items.film: Two cameras, or two people filming each end, then cut between them.

items.title: Straw Pan Pipes
steps: Cut the straws to eight different lengths, each about 1 cm shorter than the last.
Lay them side by side in order on the card strip and tape them down.
Plug the bottom end of every straw with a twist of tape.
Blow across the tops, not into them, and play up and down the row.
items.why: Blowing across the top sets the column of air inside the straw shaking. A short column shakes quickly and your ears hear that as a high note, while a long column shakes slowly and sounds low. Every wind instrument is doing this, just with cleverer ways of changing the length.
items.twist: Cut a ninth straw exactly half the length of your longest one. It plays the same note, one octave higher.
items.film: Play a tune everyone knows, however badly. That is the video.

items.title: Box Guitar
stuff: A shoebox or a strong carton
steps: Ask an adult to cut a round hole about 8 cm across in the lid.
Stretch the rubber bands round the box so they cross over the hole.
Slide a pencil under the bands on each side of the hole to lift them off the box.
Pluck each band, then slide one pencil closer to the other and pluck again.
items.why: A plucked band vibrates and pushes the air inside the box, and that is a far bigger push than the thin band could manage on its own, which is why the box makes it loud. Thick or loose bands vibrate slowly and sound low, thin or tight ones vibrate fast and sound high.
items.care: An adult cuts the hole.
items.twist: Tune the bands until you can play a scale, then work out a tune you already know.
items.film: Record it once quietly without the box, then with the box, so the difference is obvious.

items.title: Stick Sundial
stuff: A straight stick about 40 cm long
A patch of open sunny ground
steps: Push the stick upright into the ground somewhere that stays sunny all day.
On the hour, every hour, put a stone where the tip of the shadow falls and write that time on it.
Keep going all day.
The next day, tell the time using only the stones.
items.why: The shadow moves because the Earth is turning, not because the sun is travelling across the sky. The Earth turns steadily, so the shadow sweeps round steadily too. Kenya sits almost on the equator, so your midday shadow is very short compared with one in Europe on the same day.
items.twist: Mark it again in three months. The stones will not line up any more, because the sun's height in the sky has changed.
items.film: One photo an hour from the same spot, cut into a ten second time lapse.

items.title: Drip Timer
steps: Ask an adult to make a pinhole in the bottle about 2 cm up from the base.
Cover the hole with a finger, fill the bottle with water and stand it over the basin.
Let go and mark the water level on the outside every minute for ten minutes.
Use your bottle to time a race or a game.
items.why: Water pushes out of the hole harder when the bottle is full, because the weight of all the water above the hole is pressing down on it. As the level drops that push weakens and the flow slows, which is why your minute marks get closer together instead of being evenly spaced.
items.care: An adult makes the hole.
items.twist: Make a second bottle with a wider hole and a third with two holes, and see which gives the steadiest timer.
items.film: Time lapse of the level dropping past your marks.

items.title: Balancing Bird
stuff: A pen and a pencil to balance it on
steps: Draw a bird with wide wings that sweep forward, about as wide as your hand, and cut it out.
Try to balance its beak on your fingertip. It will fall straight off.
Tape one coin to the underside of each wingtip, exactly the same distance out on both sides.
Balance the beak on your fingertip again.
items.why: Something balances when the point you are holding sits directly under its centre of mass, the balance point of the whole object. The coins at the swept-forward wingtips drag that balance point forward until it sits under the beak, and because it also sits below your finger, the bird rights itself when you nudge it.
items.twist: Slide the coins backwards a centimetre at a time and find the exact point where it stops balancing.
items.film: Balance it on your fingertip, then on a pencil, then on your nose.

items.title: Straw Tilt Maze
stuff: A shoebox lid or card with a rim
A marble or a bean, and a pen
steps: Draw a maze on the lid with a start, a finish and two or three trap holes to avoid.
Cut the straws to length and glue them along every line as walls.
Ask an adult to help cut the trap holes out.
Put the marble at the start and tilt the lid with both hands to steer it.
items.why: Tilting does not push the marble sideways at all. It stops gravity pulling straight into the board, so part of the pull now runs along the surface instead. The steeper you tilt, the bigger that part is, and the faster the marble gets away from you.
items.twist: Time your best run, then swap mazes with someone else and time theirs.
items.film: Camera above the maze, hands in shot, one attempt with no cuts.

items.title: Rain Gauge
stuff: A ruler and a permanent marker
steps: Ask an adult to cut the top third off the bottle.
Put a few stones in the base so the wind cannot knock it over, pour water in until it just covers them, and mark that line as zero.
Mark every centimetre above the zero line with the ruler.
Turn the cut top upside down into the bottle as a funnel, and stand it outside away from walls and trees.
items.why: The funnel and the body are the same width, so every millimetre of rain that lands on the opening gives you a millimetre of depth in the bottle. That is why the sides must be straight. The stones and the starting water stop it blowing over and stop the first drops vanishing into a rounded base.
items.care: An adult does the cutting.
items.twist: Read it every morning for a month and draw a bar chart. Compare your numbers with the forecast.
items.film: A quick weather report to camera each morning with your reading.

items.title: Newspaper Stool
stuff: A square of stiff cardboard for the seat
steps: Roll each sheet tightly from one corner into a tube about as thick as your thumb, and tape it.
Cut every tube to the same length, about 25 cm.
Stand them upright in a bundle, packed as tightly as they will go, and tape a band hard round the top, the middle and the bottom.
Tape the cardboard on top, test it with a bag of shopping, then sit down carefully.
items.why: One paper tube standing upright carries a surprising load, because the force runs straight down the paper instead of bending it, and paper is weak in bending but strong end on. Bundle thirty together and they hold each other upright, so none of them can buckle sideways.
items.care: Test it with something heavy before you sit on it, and always put it on flat ground.
items.twist: Pull tubes out one at a time until it collapses, and you will know how many tubes one person weighs.
items.film: Sit down slowly on camera. Either way it is a good video.

items.title: Finger-Knit Friendship Bracelet
stuff: 1 ball of cotton or thick yarn
Scissors — an adult does the cutting
A door handle or a friend's finger to anchor the first loops
steps: Make a slip knot and slide it over two fingers, leaving a short tail.
Take the yarn behind your fingers, then bring it to the front between them.
Loop the yarn over the first finger, then over the second, like a figure of eight.
Lift the bottom loop on each finger up and over the top loop, then let it drop at the back.
Keep looping and lifting until the bracelet is long enough to wrap your wrist.
Slide the stitches off, tie the two ends together, and ask an adult to trim the tails.
items.why: Each loop you lift passes over the new loop and locks it in place. When you do this again and again, the locked loops line up into a soft flat band. This is the same idea as knitting: new loops pulling through old ones turn a single thread into fabric.
items.care: Only an adult cuts the yarn, and keep the scissors closed when you are not using them.
items.twist: Change to a second colour halfway and see the stripe appear. Then teach a friend the pattern.

items.title: Crochet Chain Bookmark
stuff: A 4 mm or 5 mm crochet hook
Scissors — an adult does the cutting
steps: Make a slip knot and slide it onto the hook, not too tight.
Wrap the yarn over the hook from back to front, then pull it through the loop. That is one chain.
Repeat until you have a chain about 20 cm long.
Pull the last loop all the way through to fasten off, leaving a tail.
Thread the tail on the darning needle and weave it back into the chain so it hides.
Tie a small tassel of yarn to the other end and ask an adult to trim it neatly.
items.why: A crochet chain is a row of loops where each new loop is pulled through the one before. The loop cannot open on its own because the next loop holds it shut. That lock is why a chain does not unravel when you pull it gently.
items.care: An adult cuts the yarn and trims the tassel.
items.twist: Chain 10 loops, then work back along the chain to make a thicker band. A longer chain becomes a hair tie.

items.title: Little Granny Square Coaster
stuff: A 4 mm or 5 mm crochet hook
Scissors — an adult does the cutting
steps: Chain 4 stitches and join the last to the first with a slip stitch to make a small ring.
Work 3 treble stitches into the ring, then chain 1. Repeat this set three more times, then join.
Change to your second colour and work treble stitches into the gaps between the groups to make the square bigger.
Keep going round with 3 trebles per gap and 2 chains at each corner until the square is as wide as your palm.
Fasten off, then use the darning needle to weave both tails into the back.
Ask an adult to trim the ends, then press the coaster flat under a heavy book for an hour.
items.why: Treble stitches are tall stitches: you wrap the yarn over the hook first, so each stitch uses more yarn and stands higher. Working them into the gaps of the round below makes the fabric grow outwards in a flat square, not a tube.
items.care: An adult does all the cutting with the scissors.
items.twist: Make four squares and join them edge to edge with the darning needle to start a small blanket. Change colour every round for a rainbow.

items.title: Pom-Pom Yarn Keyring
stuff: Two rounds of cardboard about the size of a mug base
Scissors — an adult does the cutting
A split ring or a short piece of string for the loop
steps: Cut a piece of yarn about 30 cm long and set it aside for tying later.
Wrap the yarn round the two cardboard rounds together until the middle is thick and even.
Ask an adult to cut between the two rounds all the way round, straight through the yarn.
Slide the reserved yarn between the two boards and tie it tightly round the middle of the bundle.
Pull the cardboard away carefully and fluff the pom-pom into a ball.
Ask an adult to trim any long ends so the pom-pom is neat, then thread the split ring through the tie.
items.why: When you cut all the wrapped strands, each short piece only stays in place because the middle is tied. The tight middle tie squeezes the strands together, and the cut ends spring outwards, which is what makes the round fluffy shape.
items.care: Only an adult cuts between the cardboard rounds and trims the pom-pom.
items.twist: Make three pom-poms in different sizes and tie them in a row for a keyring charm. Use the same wool colour as a scarf to match.

items.title: Crochet Flower Hair Clip
stuff: Small amounts of yarn in two colours
A plain hair clip or bobby pin
Scissors — an adult does the cutting
steps: Chain 4 and join into a ring with a slip stitch.
Work 3 treble stitches into the ring, then chain 1. Repeat until you have 5 petals, then join to the first stitch.
Fasten off, leaving a long tail for sewing.
Use the tail and the darning needle to sew the flower onto the hair clip, going through the metal twice.
Add a second colour as a small centre by sewing a few loops over the middle.
Ask an adult to trim the ends and check the flower is fixed tightly.
items.why: Each group of treble stitches fans out from one point, so the middle stays narrow and the outside opens wide. Five of these groups arranged in a circle make a five-petal flower. The sewing tail is what holds the yarn to the clip, not the hook.
items.care: An adult cuts the yarn and trims the ends.
items.twist: Make a flower in three sizes and sew them together as a brooch. Try thinner yarn and a smaller hook for a tiny flower.

items.title: Simple Crochet Headband
stuff: A 4 mm or 5 mm crochet hook
A tape measure or a piece of string
Scissors — an adult does the cutting
steps: Measure round your head and write the number down. Subtract 4 cm so the band stretches to fit.
Chain enough stitches to reach that length.
Work one row of double crochet along the chain.
Keep working rows of double crochet, turning at the end of each row, until the band is about 6 cm wide.
Lay the two short ends together and join them with slip stitches to make a ring.
Weave in the tails and ask an adult to trim them.
items.why: Double crochet stitches are shorter and denser than trebles, so rows of them build a firm stretchy strip. Crochet fabric can stretch sideways because the loops can open and close, which is why the band is made a little smaller than your head.
items.care: An adult does the cutting and trims the woven-in ends.
items.twist: Work every second row in a second colour for stripes. Add a flower from the other card and sew it on the side.

items.title: Yarn-Wrapped Pen Pot
stuff: A clean tin, plastic cup or small box
Leftover yarn in two or three colours
Glue stick or a little white glue
Scissors — an adult does the cutting
steps: Wash and dry the tin so there is no label or oil left on it.
Put a thin line of glue around the bottom edge.
Press the end of the yarn into the glue and start wrapping it round and round, pushing each loop up against the last.
When you want to change colour, glue the new end over the old and carry on wrapping.
Cover the whole tin up to the rim, then glue the last end down neatly.
Ask an adult to trim loose threads, then leave the pot to dry before using it.
items.why: Winding yarn in tight side-by-side loops covers the shiny surface and makes it soft to hold. The glue only holds the loose ends, while the loops hold each other by friction, which is why the wrap stays put once it is packed closely.
items.care: An adult trims the yarn with scissors. Use a tin with a smooth rim so you do not cut your hand.
items.twist: Wrap a pencil holder for your desk, or wrap a jar and use it to keep hair bands tidy. Try wrapping in diagonal stripes instead of straight rings.

items.title: Tiny Crochet Heart
stuff: Small amount of red or pink yarn
Scissors — an adult does the cutting
steps: Chain 4 and join into a ring with a slip stitch.
Work 3 treble stitches, 3 double crochet, 1 treble, then 3 double crochet and 3 treble to go round the ring.
Slip stitch into the ring to close and fasten off, leaving a long tail.
Pull the tail gently with the darning needle to shape the dip at the top of the heart.
Weave the tail into the back of the heart and hide it.
Ask an adult to trim the end, then sew the heart to a bag or a card.
items.why: The heart shape comes from working different stitch heights around one ring. Tall trebles at the two outer edges make the rounded lobes, and the shorter stitches between them make the dip. Pulling the middle tail tight closes the pointed bottom.
items.care: An adult does the cutting and trimming.
items.twist: Make two hearts and sew them back to back with a little stuffing of yarn scraps for a small hanging decoration.

items.title: Crochet Phone Pouch
stuff: A 4 mm or 5 mm crochet hook
A phone to measure against, or a ruler
A button and a short piece of yarn for the loop
Scissors — an adult does the cutting
steps: Measure the width of the phone and chain enough stitches to reach that width plus 1 cm.
Work rows of double crochet until the piece is twice as tall as the phone.
Fold the piece in half and join the two side edges with slip stitches to make a pouch.
Make a loop of about 12 chains and sew it to the top of the front flap.
Sew the button on the back so the loop can hook over it.
Weave in all the tails and ask an adult to trim them.
items.why: Joining the side edges with slip stitches turns a flat rectangle into a tube with a closed base, which is how most crochet bags and pouches are made. Double crochet is dense, so the fabric protects the phone from knocks and dust.
items.care: An adult does the cutting and trims the woven ends. Keep the pouch away from water.
items.twist: Add a long strap of chains to wear it over your shoulder. Sew a small heart from the other card onto the front.
